questions.stem: A 27-year-old female with a history of asthma presents to the ER in severe respiratory distress. Her fiancé states that she has been intubated in the ICU twice. This episode started 30 minutes ago and they came straight to the ED after her rescue medications failed to help. Her vitals are currently BP 126/86 mmHg, RR 24/min and O2 Saturation 84% on 100% O2 via non-rebreather with continuous albuterol. While nursing staff prepare methylprednisolone, magnesium, and BIPAP, you determine intubation is likely necessary. Which of the following is the preferred induction agent for this patient?
questions.stemHtml: A 27-year-old female with a history of asthma presents to the ER in severe respiratory distress. Her fiancé states that she has been intubated in the ICU twice. This episode started 30 minutes ago and they came straight to the ED after her rescue medications failed to help. Her vitals are currently BP 126/86 mmHg, RR 24/min and O2 Saturation 84% on 100% O2 via non-rebreather with continuous albuterol. While nursing staff prepare methylprednisolone, magnesium, and BIPAP, you determine intubation is likely necessary. Which of the following is the preferred induction agent for this patient?
questions.solution: Correct Option C - Ketamine: The preferred agent in respiratory failure in the setting of asthma exacerbation is ketamine (1-2 mg/kg IVP). Ketamine is a dissociative anesthetic that also carries bronchodilator effects that have reported benefits in acute asthma. Ketamine preserves respiratory drive. It has a quick onset of action and analgesic properties, which makes it a good choice for "awake" intubation attempts , used when laryngoscopy is performed on a patient who is moderately sedated and topically anesthetized but not paralyzed due to concerns about a difficult airway. Adverse effects may include increased airway secretions and emergence reactions. Proper sedation should be maintained after intubation to prevent emergence reactions. Other induction agents may be used however the bronchodilation from ketamine makes this a good option. Caution should be exercised as ketamine can cause increased secretions. Incorrect Options: Option A - Etomidate: Etomidate may be used however the bronchodilation from ketamine makes this a good option. Option B - Midazolam: Midazolam is less effective than ketamine. Option D - Lorazepam: Lorazepam is also less effective. @Neet_pg_bot
questions.solutionHtml:
Correct Option C - Ketamine:

  • The preferred agent in respiratory failure in the setting of asthma exacerbation is ketamine (1-2 mg/kg IVP).
  • Ketamine is a dissociative anesthetic that also carries bronchodilator effects that have reported benefits in acute asthma. Ketamine preserves respiratory drive.
  • It has a quick onset of action and analgesic properties, which makes it a good choice for "awake" intubation attempts, used when laryngoscopy is performed on a patient who is moderately sedated and topically anesthetized but not paralyzed due to concerns about a difficult airway.
  • Adverse effects may include increased airway secretions and emergence reactions. Proper sedation should be maintained after intubation to prevent emergence reactions.
  • Other induction agents may be used however the bronchodilation from ketamine makes this a good option. Caution should be exercised as ketamine can cause increased secretions.

Incorrect Options:

Option A - Etomidate: Etomidate may be used however the bronchodilation from ketamine makes this a good option.

Option B - Midazolam: Midazolam is less effective than ketamine.

Option D - Lorazepam: Lorazepam is also less effective.

questions.stem: A 65-year-old female presents with 2 days of fatigue. She has a history of hypertension and reports compliance with home medications. The patient reports beginning a new exercise program 4 weeks ago that her grandson recommended to her. She reports taking oil of wintergreen to manage her muscle aches since increasing her activity level. Temperature is 99.5ºF, pulse is 99 bpm, RR is 26/min, BP is 148/86 mm of Hg, and SpO2 is 97% on room air. She has mild generalized abdominal tenderness on exam. Arterial blood gas is pH 7.31, PaCO2 28, PaO2 89, and HCO3 15. Urine drug screen is negative. What will help make the diagnosis?
questions.stemHtml: A 65-year-old female presents with 2 days of fatigue. She has a history of hypertension and reports compliance with home medications. The patient reports beginning a new exercise program 4 weeks ago that her grandson recommended to her. She reports taking oil of wintergreen to manage her muscle aches since increasing her activity level. Temperature is 99.5ºF, pulse is 99 bpm, RR is 26/min, BP is 148/86 mm of Hg, and SpO2 is 97% on room air. She has mild generalized abdominal tenderness on exam. Arterial blood gas is pH 7.31, PaCO2 28, PaO2 89, and HCO3 15. Urine drug screen is negative. What will help make the diagnosis?
questions.solution: Correct Option D - Serum salicylate level: Salicylate toxicity classically presents as a mixed acid base disorder , as noted in this patient’s workup. She has metabolic acidosis with low bicarbonate (HCO3) and pH 7.31 with respiratory alkalosis . Salicylates, the active ingredient in oil of wintergreen (methyl salicylate), cause uncoupling of oxidative phosphorylation , leading to low serum bicarbonate levels. In an attempt to correct this metabolic acidosis and maintain a steady state, the body begins to hyperventilate to “blow off” CO2. This patient is tachypneic, indicated by a respiratory rate of 26. Her vital signs and blood gas suggest salicylate toxicity. A serum salicylate level will help make the diagnosis. Incorrect Options: Options A - Abdominal ultrasound: Abdominal pain in an elderly patient is a common complaint, and it carries a high likelihood of morbidity. Evaluation of the patient’s abdominal pain is prudent. However, this patient has no specific abdominal exam findings (e.g., Murphy’s sign) warranting evaluation with imaging. Option B - Chest X-ray: Although the patient has vital sign abnormalities (e.g., tachypnea), there is likely more going on than can be evaluated by a chest X-ray. The patient has been self-medicating with oil of wintergreen, which is a salicylate. Her acid-base disorder in combination with the other signs point toward salicylate toxicity. Option C - Serum creatine kinase level: Increased exercise can lead to increased muscle tissue breakdown and rhabdomyolysis. Rhabdomyolysis can result in acute tubular necrosis and acute kidney failure if not managed with aggressive fluid resuscitation. A serum creatine kinase (CK) level can be obtained to assess the degree of muscle tissue breakdown. However, there is no mention of the patient looking dehydrated or having dark or bloody urine. Her application of oil of wintergreen along with her blood gas results point toward another etiology of her symptoms. @Neet_pg_bot

questions.stem: A 57-year-old male presents to the emergency room, complaining of chest pain, with a past medical history of concern for hypertension and hyperlipidemia. Vital signs are unremarkable. Initial ECG concerning left bundle branch block (LBBB). When looking through his old records, you find that previous ECGs also showed a LBBB. Which of the following criteria is not consistent with new-onset myocardial infarction?
questions.stemHtml: A 57-year-old male presents to the emergency room, complaining of chest pain, with a past medical history of concern for hypertension and hyperlipidemia. Vital signs are unremarkable. Initial ECG concerning left bundle branch block (LBBB). When looking through his old records, you find that previous ECGs also showed a LBBB. Which of the following criteria is not consistent with new-onset myocardial infarction?

options.label: A
options.text: Concordant ST elevation >1mm in leads with positive QRS complex

options.label: B
options.text: Excessively discordant ST elevation >5mm in leads with a negative QRS complex

options.label: D
options.text: Discordant ST depression >1mm in leads II and III

questions.answerText: Discordant ST depression >1mm in leads II and III
questions.solution: Correct Option D - Discordant ST depression >1mm in leads II and III: This question tests your knowledge of the Sgarbossa criteria. Acute myocardial infarction is difficult to detect when a known LBBB is present. The Sgarbossa criteria were developed after a review of electrocardiographic diagnosis of evolving MI in the presence of LBBB in 26,003 patients with AMI confirmed by cardiac enzyme studies. The data was collected in the GUSTO-1 trial. A logistical model allowed the development of a scoring system to assess the likelihood of AMI in the presence of LBBB. Each criterion is assigned a point value and a minimal score of 3 points is 90% specific for myocardial infarction. Incorrect Answers: Option A - Concordant ST elevation >1mm in leads with positive QRS complex: This ECG finding scored 5 points. Option B - Excessively discordant ST elevation >5mm in leads with a negative QRS complex: The criterion listed in answer B is to score 2 points. Option C - Concordant ST depression >1mm in V1-V3: The criteria listed in answer C is scored at 3 points. All of the above are associated with possible myocardial infarction in LBBB. Greater than or equal to 3 points has a 90% specificity for STEMI. @Neet_pg_bot

Correct Option D - Discordant ST depression >1mm in leads II and III:

The Sgarbossa criteria were developed after a review of electrocardiographic diagnosis of evolving MI in the presence of LBBB in 26,003 patients with AMI confirmed by cardiac enzyme studies. The data was collected in the GUSTO-1 trial. A logistical model allowed the development of a scoring system to assess the likelihood of AMI in the presence of LBBB. Each criterion is assigned a point value and a minimal score of 3 points is 90% specific for myocardial infarction.

Incorrect Answers:

Option A - Concordant ST elevation >1mm in leads with positive QRS complex: This ECG finding scored 5 points.

Option B - Excessively discordant ST elevation >5mm in leads with a negative QRS complex: The criterion listed in answer B is to score 2 points.

Option C - Concordant ST depression >1mm in V1-V3: The criteria listed in answer C is scored at 3 points. All of the above are associated with possible myocardial infarction in LBBB. Greater than or equal to 3 points has a 90% specificity for STEMI.

questions.stem: A cigarette smoker with a history of lower-extremity claudication is started on an ACE inhibitor for hypertension that failed to improve with lifestyle modifications. His serum Cr doubled after the initiation of the ACE inhibitor. This is suggestive of which finding?
questions.stemHtml: A cigarette smoker with a history of lower-extremity claudication is started on an ACE inhibitor for hypertension that failed to improve with lifestyle modifications. His serum Cr doubled after the initiation of the ACE inhibitor. This is suggestive of which finding?
questions.solution: Correct Option A - Significant bilateral renal artery stenosis: In bilateral renal artery stenosis, GFR is preserved by the actions of angiotensin II, afferent arteriolar vasodilation, and efferent arteriolar vasoconstriction. ACE inhibitors and angiotensin II receptor blockers blunt these responses, resulting in a decrease in GFR and an increase in serum Cr. Thiazide diuretics and calcium channel blockers are better choices for hypertensive patients with bilateral renal artery stenosis. Incorrect Options: Option B - Pheochromocytoma: Pheochromocytoma is due to hypersecretion of renin from catecholamine excess. It is not associated with a rise in serum creatinine related to the use of ACEIs. Option C - Primary aldosteronism: Primary aldosteronism is due to primary hypersecretion of aldosterone and secondary suppression of renin and angiotensin II. It is not associated with a rise in creatinine associated with ACEI therapy. Option D - Atherosclerotic emboli from the aorta: Atherosclerotic emboli of the aorta are not associated with a rise in serum creatinine with ACEI therapy. @Neet_pg_bot
questions.solutionHtml:
Correct Option A - Significant bilateral renal artery stenosis:

  • In bilateral renal artery stenosis, GFR is preserved by the actions of angiotensin II, afferent arteriolar vasodilation, and efferent arteriolar vasoconstriction.
  • ACE inhibitors and angiotensin II receptor blockers blunt these responses, resulting in a decrease in GFR and an increase in serum Cr.
  • Thiazide diuretics and calcium channel blockers are better choices for hypertensive patients with bilateral renal artery stenosis.

Incorrect Options:

Option B - Pheochromocytoma: Pheochromocytoma is due to hypersecretion of renin from catecholamine excess. It is not associated with a rise in serum creatinine related to the use of ACEIs.

Option C - Primary aldosteronism: Primary aldosteronism is due to primary hypersecretion of aldosterone and secondary suppression of renin and angiotensin II. It is not associated with a rise in creatinine associated with ACEI therapy.

Option D - Atherosclerotic emboli from the aorta: Atherosclerotic emboli of the aorta are not associated with a rise in serum creatinine with ACEI therapy.

questions.stem: A 56-year-old male presents to the emergency department via ambulance. The patient was reported to have had vomiting, followed by a sudden syncopal episode while walking that was witnessed by his wife. The paramedics were called and found the patient with shallow breaths and hypoxic at 76% O2 saturation so the patient was intubated immediately. The patient was brought into the emergency department. HR is 56/min and blood pressure is 216/100 mmHg. Pupils are pinpoint, fixed, and non-reactive. The patient has a GCS of 3. CT head was ordered, demonstrating a massive pontine hemorrhage and vasogenic edema. Which of the following is most likely true regarding his neurological exam?
questions.stemHtml: A 56-year-old male presents to the emergency department via ambulance. The patient was reported to have had vomiting, followed by a sudden syncopal episode while walking that was witnessed by his wife. The paramedics were called and found the patient with shallow breaths and hypoxic at 76% O2 saturation so the patient was intubated immediately. The patient was brought into the emergency department. HR is 56/min and blood pressure is 216/100 mmHg. Pupils are pinpoint, fixed, and non-reactive. The patient has a GCS of 3. CT head was ordered, demonstrating a massive pontine hemorrhage and vasogenic edema. Which of the following is most likely true regarding his neurological exam?

options.label: A
options.text: Oculocephalic (doll’s eye) testing will demonstrate eye movement in the direction of the head when the head is turned.

options.label: B
options.text: Oculovestibular (cold water caloric) testing will demonstrate fixed gaze without deviation

questions.answerText: Oculovestibular (cold water caloric) testing will demonstrate fixed gaze without deviation
questions.solution: Correct Option B - Oculovestibular (cold water caloric) testing will demonstrate fixed gaze without deviation: With a cold caloric stimulus, the column of endolymph nearest the middle ear falls due to increased density. This produces horizontal nystagmus with the fast phase directed away from the stimulated ear. A warm stimulus produces the opposite effect, nystagmus directed toward the stimulated ear (a mnemonic is COWS, meaning cold opposite, warm same). The mnemonic COWS is helpful, representing “Cold: Opposite and Warm: Same.” This should only be done with those without cervical injury as well as with the head of the bed at 30 degrees. Incorrect Options: Option A - Oculocephalic (doll’s eye) testing will demonstrate eye movement in the direction of the head when the head is turned: In the oculocephalic maneuver (or doll's eyes), the head is abruptly rotated from one side to the other in the horizontal plane. When the oculocephalic reflex is present (positive doll's eyes), the eyes turn in the opposite direction to the head, as if the patient is maintaining visual fixation on a single point in space. In a normal brain, an oculocephalic reflex is suppressed. This reflex is not tested in conscious patients. The cervical spine must be cleared before performing this maneuver. Option C - Downward-going toes on Babinski: A downward-going Babinski is a normal result of the exam. An upward-going toe on the exam demonstrates a possible upper motor neuron lesion. Option D - Diffuse hyporeflexia on extremities: Hyporeflexia is nonspecific, however, it may demonstrate a lower motor neuron lesion. @Neet_pg_bot

  • A warm stimulus produces the opposite effect, nystagmus directed toward the stimulated ear (a mnemonic is COWS, meaning cold opposite, warm same). The mnemonic COWS is helpful, representing “Cold: Opposite and Warm: Same.”
  • This should only be done with those without cervical injury as well as with the head of the bed at 30 degrees.

Incorrect Options:

Option A - Oculocephalic (doll’s eye) testing will demonstrate eye movement in the direction of the head when the head is turned: In the oculocephalic maneuver (or doll's eyes), the head is abruptly rotated from one side to the other in the horizontal plane. When the oculocephalic reflex is present (positive doll's eyes), the eyes turn in the opposite direction to the head, as if the patient is maintaining visual fixation on a single point in space. In a normal brain, an oculocephalic reflex is suppressed. This reflex is not tested in conscious patients. The cervical spine must be cleared before performing this maneuver.

Option C - Downward-going toes on Babinski:  A downward-going Babinski is a normal result of the exam. An upward-going toe on the exam demonstrates a possible upper motor neuron lesion.

questions.stem: A 56-year-old female with type 2 DM arrives in the ER complaining of a sore throat for the past day. She states it hurts her to swallow and she reports painful swelling under her jaw. She has mild pain when she moves her head around. In the ER her vitals are BP - 150/90 mmHg, HR - 102/min, RR - 18/min, Temperature - 100.5°F, O2 saturation - 99%. On examination, you note mild pharyngeal erythema with a few exudates, tender submandibular adenopathy, and clear lungs. She has mild discomfort when you range her neck and her voice is slightly muffled. She is not drooling and appears in NAD. What is the appropriate workup for this patient?
questions.stemHtml: A 56-year-old female with type 2 DM arrives in the ER complaining of a sore throat for the past day. She states it hurts her to swallow and she reports painful swelling under her jaw. She has mild pain when she moves her head around. In the ER her vitals are BP - 150/90 mmHg, HR - 102/min, RR - 18/min, Temperature - 100.5°F, O2 saturation - 99%. On examination, you note mild pharyngeal erythema with a few exudates, tender submandibular adenopathy, and clear lungs. She has mild discomfort when you range her neck and her voice is slightly muffled. She is not drooling and appears in NAD. What is the appropriate workup for this patient?

options.label: A
options.text: Clinically, she has strep throat based on 3/4 Centor criteria and should be treated with Augmentin and can be discharged

options.label: B
options.text: She has a viral pharyngitis and laryngitis and can be reassured, and treatment with IM dexamethasone for symptom relief

options.label: C
options.text: She needs either a lateral soft tissue X-ray or laryngoscopy to evaluate for epiglottis versus retropharyngeal abscess

options.label: D
options.text: She needs dexamethasone and ceftriaxone for suspected Ludwig's angina and admission to the oral surgery service

questions.answerText: She needs either a lateral soft tissue X-ray or laryngoscopy to evaluate for epiglottis versus retropharyngeal abscess
questions.solution: Correct Option C - She needs either a lateral soft tissue X-ray or laryngoscopy to evaluate for epiglottis versus retropharyngeal abscess: The patient exhibits a muffled voice and has pain when her neck is ranged suggests a likelihood of retropharyngeal abscess. Any patient with a muffled voice and infectious symptoms requires evaluation of their airway to rule out a source of airway narrowing and impending complete airway obstruction. Patients may need emergent prophylactic intubation to prevent this. A lateral soft tissue X-ray would show enlargement of the epiglottis or swelling of the retropharyngeal space. Although steroids and antibiotics can be given, they do not obviate the need for airway evaluation. Although this patient does meet 3/4 Centor criteria (exudates, submandibular adenopathy, fever, and lack of cough), the muffled voice and pain when ranging the neck makes this a more complicated case. Incorrect Options: Option A - Clinically, she has strep throat based on 3/4 Centor criteria and should be treated with Augmentin and can be discharged: The Centor criteria are used to assess the likelihood of streptococcal pharyngitis (strep throat). While this patient meets 3 out of 4 criteria (exudates, submandibular adenopathy, and fever), her presentation is more concerning due to the muffled voice, painful neck movement, and significant discomfort. These symptoms suggest a deeper infection rather than uncomplicated streptococcal pharyngitis. Treating with antibiotics and discharging her without further evaluation might delay the appropriate management of a potentially serious condition. Option B - She has viral pharyngitis and laryngitis and can be reassured, and treatment with IM dexamethasone for symptom relief: This option is incorrect because the patient's symptoms and physical exam findings, such as tender submandibular adenopathy, muffled voice, and discomfort when moving her neck, are suggestive of a more serious condition than just a viral pharyngitis. The need for dexamethasone and the absence of a more thorough evaluation is not appropriate in this case. Option D - She needs dexamethasone and ceftriaxone for suspected Ludwig's angina and admission to the oral surgery service: This option is incorrect because Ludwig's angina is characterized by a rapidly progressing cellulitis involving the submandibular, sublingual, and submental spaces. While the patient does have tender submandibular adenopathy, her symptoms and examination findings do not strongly support the diagnosis of Ludwig's angina. The absence of drooling and relatively mild symptoms makes this diagnosis less likely. @Neet_pg_bot

questions.stem: A 36-year-old G3P3 female presents 5 days after an unremarkable delivery. She presents with fatigue and dyspnea on exertion. A bedside ultrasound shows decreased cardiac function. Given these findings, what is the mainstay of treatment?
questions.stemHtml: A 36-year-old G3P3 female presents 5 days after an unremarkable delivery. She presents with fatigue and dyspnea on exertion. A bedside ultrasound shows decreased cardiac function. Given these findings, what is the mainstay of treatment?
questions.solution: Correct Option B - Lasix: Postpartum cardiomyopathy , now known as peripartum cardiomyopathy or pregnancy-associated cardiomyopathy, occurs in 1/4000 pregnancies and is more common in African-American and multiparous women. Onset is usually days to weeks after delivery and ranges from mild fatigue to acute pulmonary edema . Goals of treatment include optimization of hemodynamics , relief of symptoms, and, when possible, chronic therapies that improve long-term outcomes can be implemented. Treatment is similar to other types of heart failure with left ventricular systolic dysfunction: diuretics, vasodilators, and oxygen relieves the symptoms in many cases. ACE-I are contraindicated during pregnancy due to teratogenicity . Cardiac function returns to normal in half of patients during the following 6 months. Incorrect Options: Option A - Immunosuppressive therapy: Immunosuppressive therapy is not recommended for postpartum cardiomyopathy (PCCM). Its efficacy is unclear. Option C - Digoxin: Digoxin is not first-line therapy for acute decompensated heart failure, but may be useful for control of ventricular rate in patients with atrial fibrillation who cannot achieve control with beta blockers alone. It is also used when symptoms persist, and it is considered safe during pregnancy. Option D - IV immunoglobulin (IVIG): IVIG has not shown clear clinical benefit. @Neet_pg_bot
questions.solutionHtml:
Correct Option B - Lasix:

  • Postpartum cardiomyopathy, now known as peripartum cardiomyopathy or pregnancy-associated cardiomyopathy, occurs in 1/4000 pregnancies and is more common in African-American and multiparous women.

  • Onset is usually days to weeks after delivery and ranges from mild fatigue to acute pulmonary edema.

  • Goals of treatment include optimization of hemodynamics, relief of symptoms, and, when possible, chronic therapies that improve long-term outcomes can be implemented.

  • Treatment is similar to other types of heart failure with left ventricular systolic dysfunction: diuretics, vasodilators, and oxygen relieves the symptoms in many cases.

  • ACE-I are contraindicated during pregnancy due to teratogenicity.

  • Cardiac function returns to normal in half of patients during the following 6 months.

Incorrect Options:

Option A - Immunosuppressive therapy: Immunosuppressive therapy is not recommended for postpartum cardiomyopathy (PCCM). Its efficacy is unclear.

Option C - Digoxin: Digoxin is not first-line therapy for acute decompensated heart failure, but may be useful for control of ventricular rate in patients with atrial fibrillation who cannot achieve control with beta blockers alone. It is also used when symptoms persist, and it is considered safe during pregnancy.

Option D - IV immunoglobulin (IVIG): IVIG has not shown clear clinical benefit.

questions.stem: Which drug of abuse is also a schedule III prescription medication for the treatment of narcoleptic cataplexy?
questions.stemHtml: Which drug of abuse is also a schedule III prescription medication for the treatment of narcoleptic cataplexy?
questions.solution: Correct Option D - GHB (Xyrem): Xyrem is a schedule III drug and has been approved by the FDA for the treatment of cataplexy in patients with narcolepsy . The active ingredient of Xyrem, sodium oxybate or gamma-hydroxybutyrate (GHB), is a Schedule I controlled substance. Xyrem has been associated with obtundation and clinically significant respiratory depression in adults. Xyrem is available only through a restricted program under a Risk Evaluation and Mitigation Strategy (REMS). Incorrect Options: Option A - Methamphetamine (Desoxyn): Although methamphetamine is approved for ADHD and exogenous obesity, it is a schedule II drug and is only used off-label for the treatment of narcolepsy. Option B - MDMA (Ecstasy): MDMA is undergoing clinical trials for use in PTSD and anxiety in cancer patients. Option C - Ketamine: Ketamine is used frequently in anesthesia. @Neet_pg_bot

She is now feeling better, but presents with redness of the cheeks and a rash over the extremities and trunk. questions.solution: Correct Option D - Fifth disease: Erythema infectiosum, or “fifth disease,” is a common and highly contagious disease of childhood, caused by Parvovirus B19 . Patients may be asymptomatic or may present with flu-like symptoms initially, including headaches, low-grade fevers, and a runny nose. After the prodromal symptoms, patients develop a red macular rash on their cheeks (“slapped-cheek”) that spares the perioral area and may spread to the rest of the body. By the time the rash develops, patients are no longer infectious. Patients may have flares of the rash for months after the infection, precipitated by sunlight or emotional state. Diagnosis is mostly clinical but can be confirmed with specific antibody testing to parvovirus B19 . Adults may have arthralgias or arthritis as prominent symptoms. For immunocompetent individuals, infection is usually self-limited, so no treatment is needed. In patients with sickle cell anemia or other pre-existing blood abnormalities, infection with parvovirus B19 may lead to an aplastic crisis due to inhibition of erythropoiesis . Patients may experience symptoms of severe anemia, including shortness of breath, worsening heart failure, and tachycardia. This typically resolves within a few weeks after the infection has resolved. If a woman becomes infected with Parvovirus B19 during pregnancy, the fetus can develop aplastic anemia. The result is often miscarriage due to severe hydrops fetalis . Incorrect Options: Option A - Measles: Measles is a more severe illness. The maculopapular rash begins on the head and spreads downward, becoming confluent as it progresses. Option B - Rubella: Rubella has no prodrome but produces a maculopapular rash that begins on the face and generalizes to the rest of the body. Option C - Systemic lupus erythematosus: Systemic lupus erythematosus is a multisystem autoimmune disease. It can cause a malar “butterfly” rash and other cutaneous lesions, but its presentation is inconsistent with this case. @Neet_pg_bot

questions.solution: Correct Option D - Obtain a CT of the foot and an orthopedic or podiatry consult: This is a ligamentous injury to the Lisfranc joint between the second metatarsal and the medial cuneiform. In the X-ray you can see the second metatarsal head is displaced laterally without fracture, indicating instability of the ligament. It can occur during jumping. This requires surgical reduction usually by ORIF. The degree of displacement often determines the surgical procedure performed. A CT is much better for determining the degree of injury and consultation of orthopedics or podiatry should be performed urgently. A stirrup splint will not support this injury. questions.stem: You are counselling a 61-year-old woman with a 15-year history of type-2 diabetes mellitus. Her GP referred her due to persistent hyperkalaemia for the last 2 months. She has diabetic nephropathy, diabetic retinopathy, and diabetic neuropathy. In addition, she used to take over-the-counter NSAIDs for osteoarthritic joint pains. The reason for the referral is to manage her elevated potassium that did not normalise even after following a low potassium diet, stoppage of losartan, and avoidance of NSAIDs. Clinical examination revealed a pulse of 80 beats per minute, a blood pressure of 136 /80 mmHg, and mild bilateral ankle oedema. Her most recent laboratory results show the following: Investigation Result Creatinine 1.13 mg/dL eGFR (using CKD-EPI) 64.3 mL/min/1.73m2 Sodium 138 mEq/L Potassium 5.8 mEq/L Blood PH (venous) 7.30 Blood HCO3 - (Venous) 24 mmol/L Anion gap 9 mEq/L Urine PH 5.6 Fasting glucose 162 mg/dL HbA1c 8.2 % Haemoglobin 14 g/dL Cortisol level (9 a.m.) 16 micro g/L Serum aldosterone (Supine) 2.16ng/ml Plasma renin activity (PRA) (Supine) 37.9pg/ml/hr What is the best course of treatment to be advised in this case ?

questions.solution: Correct Option C - Hydrochlorothiazide: Persistent or chronic hyperkalaemia in a patient with long-standing type-2 diabetes mellitus (DM) in the absence of a clear cause, e.g. an advanced stage of renal disease, will raise the suspicion of hyporeninemic hypoaldosteronism (HH). In such cases with chronic hyperkalaemia, patients are advised to stop using non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs), angiotensin-converting enzyme (ACE) inhibitors, or angiotensin receptor blockers (ARBs). They are also requested to decrease potassium intake. If the potassium level does not reach the target with these measures, a thiazide or loop diuretic could be added. In this patient, the most appropriate next step decision is the addition of hydrochlorothiazide. In resistant cases where diuretics fail to correct hyperkalaemia, fludrocortisone could be used with careful follow-up of sodium and potassium levels as well as any signs of hypervolaemia . It should be noted that any acute or life-threatening hyperkalaemia should be treated as an emergency with calcium gluconate, insulin, salbutamol, calcium exchange resins, diuretics, or even dialysis. Most patients with HH are asymptomatic with biochemical findings of persistent hyperkalaemia. HH is associated with normal anion gap hyperchloraemic metabolic acidosis (type IV renal tubular acidosis) that resulted from hyperkalaemia, hypoaldosteronism, and decreased renal ammonia formation. Chronic acidosis may contribute to long-term morbid conditions, including bone demineralisation . Finally, ‘hypoaldosteronism may result from disturbances in renal renin production and secretion, conversion of angiotensin I to angiotensin II, adrenal aldosterone synthesis and secretion, or abnormal responsiveness of the target tissues to aldosterone’. Incorrect Options: Option A - Aliskiren: Aliskiren is a direct renin inhibitor. In this scenario renin levels are low. So it is not indicated Option B - Calcium gluconate: Calcium Gluconate is used in emergency management of Hyperkalemia Option D - Hydrocortisone: In resistant cases where diuretics fail to correct hyperkalaemia, fludrocortisone could be used, but not Hydrocortisone @Neet_pg_bot

questions.stem: The 65-year-old male was admitted from the Emergency room with a two day history of sudden onset abnormal jerky movements involving the right arm. He had four previous admissions with hyperosmolar hyperglycaemic states in the last five years, with the most recent admission occurring two months ago. There is no prior history of seizures or abnormal jerks in the past. He has a background history of Type 2 diabetes for 15 years, hypertension, hypercholesterolemia and chronic hepatitis B. His diabetes over the past five years has been uncontrolled due to noncompliance with drugs and poor motivation, despite repeated sessions with the clinical psychologist. His current medications include insulin, metformin, atorvastatin, perindopril, amlodipine, and lamivudine. Recently, his perindopril dose was increased to 8 mg from 4 mg. He is a non smoker and denies taking alcohol or illicit drugs. On examination, his vital signs were stable. He was fully oriented and coherent. A neurological examination showed choreiform movements involving the right arm occurring at rest. The rest of his sensory, motor, cranial nerves and cerebellar examination was normal. His systemic examination was also unremarkable. His blood test showed normal full blood counts, electrolytes, renal function, thyroid function, liver function and ECG. His random blood sugar on admission was 27, serum osmolality 308 mOsm/kg and HbA1c was 13%. His MRI brain showed hyperintensity at the caudate nucleus on T1W1 and hypointensity on T2W and FLAIR images. What is the likely underlying diagnosis?

questions.solution: Correct Option B - Diabetic striatopathy: The important causes for T1 hyperintensity on MRI in the basal ganglia include diabetic striatopathy, Wilson's disease, hepatic encephalopathy, manganese toxicity and carbon monoxide poisoning. Management of Diabetic striatopathy includes improved glycaemic control and anti-chorea medications, such as haloperidol, tetrabenazine, risperidone alone or in combination with benzodiazepines such as clonazepam and diazepam. Successful treatment rates with glucose-lowering only and additional anti-chorea medications are 25.7% and 76.2%, respectively. Recovery time ranges between 2-14 days and the overall recurrence rate is 18.2%. questions.solution: Correct Option D - Apo E2 / E2 genotype synthesis with increased IDL and chylomicron concentrations: Type III hyperlipoproteinemia occurs as a consequence of elevated chylomicron and IDL (intermediate density lipoprotein) concentrations. Also known as broad beta disease or dysbetalipoproteinemia, the most common cause for this form is the presence of Apo E2/E2 genotype. It is due to cholesterol-rich VLDL (β-VLDL). Prevalence is 0.02% of the population. Apolipoprotein E (APOE) is an apoprotein found in chylomicron and IDL particles that binds to a specific receptor on liver cells and peripheral cells. It is essential for the normal catabolism of triglyceride-rich lipoprotein constituents. APOE was initially recognized for its importance in lipoprotein metabolism and cardiovascular disease. More recently, it has been studied for its role in several biological processes not directly related to lipoprotein transport, including Alzheimer's disease, immuno-regulation, and cognition. Defects in APOE result in familial dysbetalipoproteinemia, or type III hyperlipoproteinemia (HLP III), in which increased plasma cholesterol and triglycerides are the consequence of impaired clearance of chylomicron, VLDL and LDL remnants. Incorrect Options: Option A - Apo E2 / E2 genotype with increased LDL and chylomicron concentrations: This option is incorrect because the Apo E2 / E2 genotype is associated with type III hyperlipoproteinemia, but the key feature in this genotype is an accumulation of intermediate-density lipoprotein (IDL) and remnants, not necessarily increased LDL concentrations. Chylomicron concentrations can also be increased. Option B - Apo E2 / E4 genotype with increased LDL and chylomicron concentrations: This option is incorrect because it involves a combination of ApoE2 and ApoE4 genotypes, which is not a known contributor to type III hyperlipoproteinemia. Type III hyperlipoproteinemia is primarily associated with the Apo E2 / E2 genotype. Option C - Apo E4 / E4 genotype with increased LDL and chylomicron concentrations: This option is incorrect because the Apo E4 / E4 genotype is not associated with type III hyperlipoproteinemia. Instead, ApoE4 is more commonly associated with increased risk for atherosclerosis and Alzheimer's disease. @Neet_pg_bot

questions.stem: A 28-year-old woman presents after being unable to conceive for the past 12 months, seeking advice regarding the etiology of this problem. Her partner had a semen analysis with normal parameters as he previously visited a urologist for the same issue. What is the next step in investigating the cause of infertility in this patient?
questions.stemHtml: A 28-year-old woman presents after being unable to conceive for the past 12 months, seeking advice regarding the etiology of this problem. Her partner had a semen analysis with normal parameters as he previously visited a urologist for the same issue. What is the next step in investigating the cause of infertility in this patient?
questions.solution: Correct Option - Ovulation and tubal patency assessment: Inability to conceive after a period of 12 months of unprotected intercourse is defined as infertility. This requires investigation of possible female and male factor infertility. Ovulation and tubal patency investigations (ovulation tests, HSG and/or laparoscopy) are the basic female infertility investigations needed while a semen analysis is the basic male infertility investigation required. Incorrect Options: Option A - Antral Follicle Count and Karyotype: Antral follicle count is a method used to estimate ovarian reserve, but it's not the next step in investigating the cause of infertility in this case. Ovarian reserve assessment (which is mentioned in option C) could involve antral follicle count, but it's not the immediate next step. Karyotype refers to the chromosomal makeup of an individual. While karyotype analysis can be relevant in infertility cases, it's not the next step in this specific scenario where the patient has been trying to conceive for 12 months and her partner's semen analysis is normal. Option B - Diagnostic Laparoscopy and Hysteroscopy: Diagnostic laparoscopy is a surgical procedure that allows direct visualization of the pelvic organs. Hysteroscopy involves looking inside the uterus. These procedures are generally considered after other initial tests have been conducted, especially if there's a suspicion of structural abnormalities or endometriosis. However, they are not the immediate next step in a case where the partner's semen analysis is normal. Option C - Ovarian Reserve Assessment: Ovarian reserve assessment is a relevant consideration in infertility cases, as it provides information about the quantity and quality of a woman's eggs. This could include tests like measuring anti-Müllerian hormone (AMH) levels, follicle-stimulating hormone (FSH) levels, and antral follicle count. It's a reasonable option to consider, and it's an important aspect of evaluating infertility, but it's not the next step in this case. @Neet_pg_bot

questions.stem: A 20-year-old lady presented to the accident and emergency department with abdominal pain, nausea and vomiting. She has a 5-year history of type 1 diabetes with poor adherence to her therapy. Her current insulin regimen comprises insulin glargine and Novo rapid via a basal-bolus regimen. On examination she is dehydrated and breathing deeply, her blood pressure is 98/66 mmHg and her pulse is 105 bpm. Investigations- Investigation Result Normal range Plasma glucose 381.6 mg/dL < 140.4 mg/dL pH 6.9 7.35 - 7.45 pCO2 3.2 kPa 4.7 - 6 pO2 12.1 kPa 9.5 - 13 kPa Serum bicarbonate 5.2 mmol/L 22 - 27 mmol/L Haemoglobin 15.9 g/dL 12 - 16 g/dL WBC 21.1 x 109L 4 - 11 x 109/L Which of the following is a feature of the pathophysiology of diabetic ketoacidosis?

Which of the following is a feature of the pathophysiology of diabetic ketoacidosis?

options.label: B
options.text: Acidaemia is the primary cause of intracellular potassium loss

options.label: C
options.text: Hepatic glucose production reaches a plateau within 4 hours of insulin withdrawal

options.label: D
options.text: Hepatic glucose production rises gradually over the first 6 - 8 hours following insulin withdrawal

questions.answerText: Hepatic glucose production reaches a plateau within 4 hours of insulin withdrawal
questions.solution: Correct Options C - Hepatic glucose production reaches a plateau within 4 hours of insulin withdrawal: Diabetic ketoacidosis is an extension of the normal fasting state. Hepatic glucose production rises rapidly over the first 2 – 4 hours following insulin withdrawal reaching a plateau after around 4 hours. These changes correlate with the initial acute rise in glucagon concentrations, with other counter-regulatory hormones being little affected initially. Basal hepatic glucose production in DKA is approximately twice that in stable diabetic patients, with a much smaller decrease in peripheral glucose utilization. Lack of insulin switches fatty acid metabolism. Beta-hydroxybutyrate is produced in excess and is subsequently metabolized to acetoacetate which is detected in urine ketone analysis by dipstick testing. Glucagon levels also further enhance fatty acid oxidation. Incorrect Options: Option A - Acetoacetate is metabolized to beta-hydroxybutyrate: This statement is incorrect. In reality, beta-hydroxybutyrate is metabolized to acetoacetate, not the other way around. Diabetic ketoacidosis (DKA) is characterized by the production of ketone bodies, including beta-hydroxybutyrate and acetoacetate, due to the breakdown of fatty acids in the absence of sufficient insulin. Option B - Acidaemia is the primary cause of intracellular potassium loss: This statement is incorrect. While it's true that acidemia (low blood pH) can lead to intracellular potassium shifts, the primary cause of intracellular potassium loss in DKA is insulin deficiency. In the absence of insulin, potassium shifts from the intracellular space to the extracellular space, leading to hyperkalemia (high blood potassium levels) in the early stages of DKA. It's the treatment of DKA with insulin that can reverse this potassium shift. Option D - Hepatic glucose production rises gradually over the first 6 - 8 hours following insulin withdrawal: This statement is incorrect. Hepatic glucose production actually rises rapidly over the first 2 - 4 hours following insulin withdrawal in DKA, not gradually over 6 - 8 hours. After reaching a peak, it plateaus around 4 hours. The rapid rise in hepatic glucose production is a result of the increased secretion of counter-regulatory hormones like glucagon, which occurs in response to the lack of insulin. @Neet_pg_bot
questions.solutionHtml:
Correct Options C - Hepatic glucose production reaches a plateau within 4 hours of insulin withdrawal:

  • Diabetic ketoacidosis is an extension of the normal fasting state. Hepatic glucose production rises rapidly over the first 2 – 4 hours following insulin withdrawal reaching a plateau after around 4 hours. These changes correlate with the initial acute rise in glucagon concentrations, with other counter-regulatory hormones being little affected initially. Basal hepatic glucose production in DKA is approximately twice that in stable diabetic patients, with a much smaller decrease in peripheral glucose utilization. Lack of insulin switches fatty acid metabolism. Beta-hydroxybutyrate is produced in excess and is subsequently metabolized to acetoacetate which is detected in urine ketone analysis by dipstick testing. Glucagon levels also further enhance fatty acid oxidation.

Incorrect Options:

Option A - Acetoacetate is metabolized to beta-hydroxybutyrate: This statement is incorrect. In reality, beta-hydroxybutyrate is metabolized to acetoacetate, not the other way around. Diabetic ketoacidosis (DKA) is characterized by the production of ketone bodies, including beta-hydroxybutyrate and acetoacetate, due to the breakdown of fatty acids in the absence of sufficient insulin.

Option B - Acidaemia is the primary cause of intracellular potassium loss: This statement is incorrect. While it's true that acidemia (low blood pH) can lead to intracellular potassium shifts, the primary cause of intracellular potassium loss in DKA is insulin deficiency. In the absence of insulin, potassium shifts from the intracellular space to the extracellular space, leading to hyperkalemia (high blood potassium levels) in the early stages of DKA. It's the treatment of DKA with insulin that can reverse this potassium shift.

Option D - Hepatic glucose production rises gradually over the first 6 - 8 hours following insulin withdrawal: This statement is incorrect. Hepatic glucose production actually rises rapidly over the first 2 - 4 hours following insulin withdrawal in DKA, not gradually over 6 - 8 hours. After reaching a peak, it plateaus around 4 hours. The rapid rise in hepatic glucose production is a result of the increased secretion of counter-regulatory hormones like glucagon, which occurs in response to the lack of insulin.

questions.stem: A 32-year-old female presents with complaints of a recent cough and shortness of breath for the last 4 days. The patient suffers from intermittent urinary tract infections, which are managed with therapy as needed with nitrofurantoin. You suspect nitrofurantoin is the cause of her likely drug-induced pulmonary symptoms. Which of the following statements is accurate regarding acute nitrofurantoin-induced pulmonary complications?
questions.stemHtml: A 32-year-old female presents with complaints of a recent cough and shortness of breath for the last 4 days. The patient suffers from intermittent urinary tract infections, which are managed with therapy as needed with nitrofurantoin. You suspect nitrofurantoin is the cause of her likely drug-induced pulmonary symptoms. Which of the following statements is accurate regarding acute nitrofurantoin-induced pulmonary complications?

options.label: A
options.text: The patient is more likely to have pulmonary vasculitis with eosinophilia

options.label: B
options.text: The pulmonary reaction seen in this patient is a less common pulmonary reaction associated with nitrofurantoin

options.label: C
options.text: The patient is more likely to have diffuse interstitial fibrosis

options.label: D
options.text: Treatment with corticosteroids has shown a benefit in recovery.

questions.answerText: The patient is more likely to have pulmonary vasculitis with eosinophilia
questions.solution: Correct Option A - The patient is more likely to have pulmonary vasculitis with eosinophilia: Pulmonary vasculitis with eosinophilia is typical of the acute form of nitrofurantoin-induced pulmonary toxicity, with hypersensitivity pneumonitis. Incorrect Options: Option B - The pulmonary reaction seen in this patient is a less common pulmonary reaction associated with nitrofurantoin: The chronic, rather than acute, form of nitrofurantoin pulmonary toxicity is less common. Option C - The patient is more likely to have diffuse interstitial fibrosis : Nitrofurantoin-induced pulmonary complication presents in acute and chronic forms. This patient likely has an acute form of pulmonary injury. The less common chronic form is associated with diffuse interstitial fibrosis, is present for at least 1 month or more, and often presents with dyspnea, coughing, and chest pain. Option D - Treatment with corticosteroids has shown a benefit in recovery: Corticosteroid therapy has shown no benefit in the treatment of nitrofurantoin-induced lung injury, with discontinuation of the drug the only action which has shown benefit. @Neet_pg_bot
questions.solutionHtml:
Correct Option A - The patient is more likely to have pulmonary vasculitis with eosinophilia:

  • Pulmonary vasculitis with eosinophilia is typical of the acute form of nitrofurantoin-induced pulmonary toxicity, with hypersensitivity pneumonitis.

Incorrect Options:

Option B - The pulmonary reaction seen in this patient is a less common pulmonary reaction associated with nitrofurantoin: The chronic, rather than acute, form of nitrofurantoin pulmonary toxicity is less common.

Option C - The patient is more likely to have diffuse interstitial fibrosis: Nitrofurantoin-induced pulmonary complication presents in acute and chronic forms. This patient likely has an acute form of pulmonary injury. The less common chronic form is associated with diffuse interstitial fibrosis, is present for at least 1 month or more, and often presents with dyspnea, coughing, and chest pain.

Option D - Treatment with corticosteroids has shown a benefit in recovery: Corticosteroid therapy has shown no benefit in the treatment of nitrofurantoin-induced lung injury, with discontinuation of the drug the only action which has shown benefit.

questions.stem: A 78-year-old female with cellulitis is admitted overnight with shortness of breath. The excited admitting intern sends a battery of tests, including urinalysis and urine culture. You get a call at midnight asking if the patient should be started on antibiotics for possible UTI. Urine culture is in process. Urinalysis reports reveal the following: White cell count 2-5 cells/hpf Epithelial cells: many Bacteria: + Which of the following is an indication for the treatment of asymptomatic bacteriuria?
questions.stemHtml:
A 78-year-old female with cellulitis is admitted overnight with shortness of breath. The excited admitting intern sends a battery of tests, including urinalysis and urine culture. You get a call at midnight asking if the patient should be started on antibiotics for possible UTI.
Urine culture is in process. Urinalysis reports reveal the following:
White cell count 2-5 cells/hpf
Epithelial cells: many
Bacteria: +
Which of the following is an indication for the treatment of asymptomatic bacteriuria?

options.label: B
options.text: Prior to transurethral resection of the prostate

options.label: C
options.text: Elderly women with an indwelling Foley catheter to prevent sepsis

questions.answerText: Prior to transurethral resection of the prostate
questions.solution: Correct Option B - Prior to transurethral resection of the prostate : Indications to treat asymptomatic bacteriuria include pregnancy, transurethral prostate resection or urologic procedures where mucosal bleeding is a possibility, and within the first 3 months of renal transplants. Incorrect Options: Option A - Women of childbearing age: There is no indication to treat women of childbearing age with asymptomatic bacteriuria. Option C - Elderly women with an indwelling Foley catheter to prevent sepsis: If this was a sample from an elderly woman with an indwelling Foley catheter, the bacteria in the urinalysis would be likely secondary to colonization. The urine sample given here was not a good sample since it contains many epithelial cells. Routine urine testing is not recommended unless the patient has symptoms or any other reason to suggest a UTI. A clean catch midstream sample is ideal for urinalysis; if it is a true infection, pyuria should be significant (>10/microL). In this specimen, the bacteria is likely secondary to colonization since there are very few white cells. Option D - Nursing home residents: There is no indication to treat nursing home residents with asymptomatic bacteriuria. @Neet_pg_bot

Correct Option B - Prior to transurethral resection of the prostate:

  • Indications to treat asymptomatic bacteriuria include pregnancy, transurethral prostate resection or urologic procedures where mucosal bleeding is a possibility, and within the first 3 months of renal transplants.

Incorrect Options:

Option A - Women of childbearing age: There is no indication to treat women of childbearing age with asymptomatic bacteriuria.

Option C - Elderly women with an indwelling Foley catheter to prevent sepsis: If this was a sample from an elderly woman with an indwelling Foley catheter, the bacteria in the urinalysis would be likely secondary to colonization. The urine sample given here was not a good sample since it contains many epithelial cells. Routine urine testing is not recommended unless the patient has symptoms or any other reason to suggest a UTI. A clean catch midstream sample is ideal for urinalysis; if it is a true infection, pyuria should be significant (>10/microL). He is also found to be in a state of profound diabetic ketoacidosis. On an exam, the patient has the following vital signs: temperature 38℃, blood pressure 136/86 mmHg, heart rate 102 beats per minute, and respiratory rate 24 breaths per minute. Additional findings include left periorbital edema and palatal eschars. The remainder of the physical examination is unremarkable. questions.solution: Correct Option B - Amphotericin B (lipid formulation): This patient is presenting with typical signs and symptoms of rhinocerebral mucormycosis. The lipid formulation of amphotericin B is commonly administered initially in order to gain control of this aggressive infection. The lipid formulation is preferable in order to achieve a higher loading dose faster in comparison to the deoxycholate formulation. The patient may subsequently undergo step-down therapy with oral posaconazole in addition to measures such as surgical procedures or hyperbaric oxygen treatment. Incorrect Options: Option A - Amphotericin B (deoxycholate): The deoxycholate formulation has additional toxicities that are primarily renal in nature. In addition, it is more difficult to obtain a higher level in comparison with the lipid formulation. Option C - Voriconazole: Voriconazole does not possess activity against mucormycosis species. Option D - Fluconazole: Fluconazole has no activity against mucormycosis. @Neet_pg_bot

In these patients, blood samples must be obtained for culture and appropriate antimicrobial and steroid therapy must be given prior to lumbar puncture or CT. questions.stem: Which of the following is the appropriate utilization of p24 antigen testing?
questions.stemHtml: Which of the following is the appropriate utilization of p24 antigen testing?

options.label: A
options.text: As testing for HIV positivity during the acute phase

options.label: B
options.text: For HIV testing in children 2 years of age and younger

options.label: D
options.text: As a component of fourth-generation HIV enzyme immunoassays

questions.answerText: As a component of fourth-generation HIV enzyme immunoassays
questions.solution: Correct Option D - As a component of fourth-generation HIV enzyme immunoassays : The fourth-generation HIV enzyme immunoassay is a combination antibody/antigen test, and p24 antigen testing is a component of this assay. In modern HIV testing, this is the most common utilization of p24 antigen testing. Incorrect Options: Option A - As testing for HIV positivity during the acute phase: It is no longer recommended to use p24 antigen testing universally as a means of diagnosing HIV infection during the acute phase, as this practice has been gradually replaced with HIV RNA testing using qualitative and quantitative assays. As a general rule, the purpose of HIV RNA qualitative testing such as NAAT is simply to determine the presence of HIV RNA. This method usually has a threshold of detection of 90 viral copies/mL. By comparison, quantitative assays are used to determine a viral load and are designed to follow the patient once a diagnosis has been made. questions.stem: While performing a hospital epidemiological study, your hospital group is considering implementing patient screening for MRSA carriage at the time of hospital admission in order to reduce the incidence of the infection in the hospital through prompt contact precaution protocols. Which of the following is consistent with the current literature on screening for drug-resistant bacteria on admission?
questions.stemHtml: While performing a hospital epidemiological study, your hospital group is considering implementing patient screening for MRSA carriage at the time of hospital admission in order to reduce the incidence of the infection in the hospital through prompt contact precaution protocols. Which of the following is consistent with the current literature on screening for drug-resistant bacteria on admission?

options.label: A
options.text: In several large studies, screening has resulted in a decrease in the transmission of methicillin-resistant staph aureus (MRSA).

options.label: B
options.text: Screening results in a decrease in the transmission of vancomycin-resistant enterococcus (VRE).

options.label: C
options.text: Most patients who tested positive for methicillin-resistant bacteria did not receive antibiotic treatment or undergo contact isolation precautions for 3-5 days post-hospital admission.

options.label: D
options.text: The results of each study are variable, and no definite conclusions can be drawn regarding universal patient screening.

questions.answerText: Most patients who tested positive for methicillin-resistant bacteria did not receive antibiotic treatment or undergo contact isolation precautions for 3-5 days post-hospital admission.
questions.solution: Correct Option C - Most patients who tested positive for methicillin-resistant bacteria did not receive antibiotic treatment or undergo contact isolation precautions for 3-5 days post hospital admission: MRSA is among the few hospital-acquired infections that have been implicated in nearly every type of infection, including the leading cause of surgical site infections. Risk factors for developing MRSA during admission include colonization with MRSA, recent antibiotic therapy, hemodialysis, prolonged hospitalization, and proximity to other patients infected with the organism. In theory, screening for MRSA and other drug-resistant organisms on admission should identify patients who are colonized so they can undergo treatment, and contact isolation precautions may be ordered. However, in multiple large well-designed clinical trials, most patients who tested positive for MRSA and VRE did not receive antibiotic treatment or undergo contact isolation precautions for 3-5 days after hospital admission. Incorrect Options: Option A - In several large studies, screening has resulted in a decrease in the transmission of methicillin-resistant staph aureus (MRSA): Initiation of contact precautions at this point has no impact on the reduction in the transmission of antibiotic-resistant bacteria. Option D - The results of each study are variable, and no definite conclusions can be drawn regarding universal patient screening: Due to the lag in isolation precautions and implementation of appropriate antibiotic therapy (i.e. vancomycin, linezolid), the focus should be on reinforcing standard precautions rather than implementing a hospital-wide screening program. @Neet_pg_bot

He states it began as a small, painless, and pruritic papule, but then quickly enlarged and developed a central vesicle. A biopsy is taken and the LRN polymerase chain reaction assay and ELISA tests are positive for B. anthracis. Which of the following would be the recommended therapy for this patient?
questions.stemHtml: A 23-year-old college student returned after purchasing an animal hide that caused a rash on his anterior left forearm. He states it began as a small, painless, and pruritic papule, but then quickly enlarged and developed a central vesicle. A biopsy is taken and the LRN polymerase chain reaction assay and ELISA tests are positive for B. anthracis. Which of the following would be the recommended therapy for this patient?
questions.solution: Correct Option A - Ciprofloxacin: Patients with cutaneous anthrax without systemic involvement should receive oral antimicrobial therapy with a single agent. Options include ciprofloxacin, doxycycline, levofloxacin or moxifloxacin. Patients with involvement of the head or neck, or extensive edema should be treated as patients with systemic involvement (Ciprofloxacin, meropenem, and linezolid). Incorrect Options: Option B - Trimethoprim/sulfamethoxazole (TMP/SMX): TMP/SMX would not be a viable option, as this drug lacks efficacy against Bacillus anthracis. Option C - Ciprofloxacin, meropenem, and linezolid : Ciprofloxacin, meropenem, and linezolid is the treatment regimen for systemic anthrax with suspected or proven meningitis. Option D - Amoxicillin: Amoxicillin is a potential medication for children who have penicillin-susceptible strains (minimum inhibitory concentration ≤0.5 mcg/mL). @Neet_pg_bot

questions.stemHtml: Infants who weigh &lt;2000 grams have a suboptimal immunological response to the hepatitis B vaccine. In cases in which the mother expresses positivity for hepatitis B surface antigen, which of the following is the recommended management?

options.label: A
options.text: Administer hepatitis B vaccination by 12 hours, which will count as 1 of the 3 doses in the series

options.label: B
options.text: Administer hepatitis B vaccination within 12 hours and HBIG within 7 days, with the vaccination not counting toward the 3-part series

options.label: C
options.text: Administer hepatitis B vaccination 1 month after birth, once the immunological response to the vaccine matures

options.label: D
options.text: Administer hepatitis B vaccination to the infant at any point before hospital discharge

questions.answerText: Administer hepatitis B vaccination within 12 hours and HBIG within 7 days, with the vaccination not counting toward the 3-part series
questions.solution: Correct Option B - Administer hepatitis B vaccination within 12 hours and HBIG within 7 days, with the vaccination not counting toward the 3-part series: For infants <2000 grams in weight, studies have shown a suboptimal immunological response to the administration of hepatitis B vaccination at birth. However, in special circumstances in which the mother’s hepatitis B status is not known or is positive, the hepatitis B vaccination should be administered to the infant within 12 hours regardless of weight, and HBIG should be administered within 7 days if the mother expresses positivity for hepatitis B surface antigen during laboratory testing. The vaccination is not counted toward the doses in the 3 part series, and the first official dose should be given at 1 month of age, the second at 2-3 months, and the third at 6 months. Incorrect Options: Option A - Administer hepatitis B vaccination by 12 hours, which will count as 1 of the 3 doses in the series: Although the hepatitis B vaccination should be administered within 12 hours in infants <2000 grams born to hepatitis B-positive mothers, this vaccination does not count in the 3-part series due to the suboptimal immune response in these infants. Option C - Administer hepatitis B vaccination 1 month after birth, once the immunological response to the vaccine matures: Within 12 hours, a single dose should be given. Option D - Administer hepatitis B vaccination to the infant at any point before hospital discharge: If the mother was negative for hepatitis B and the infant weighs ≥2000 grams, then the first vaccination in the series would be given at any point before hospital discharge. @Neet_pg_bot

questions.stem: A 55-year-old male kidney-transplant patient was in his usual state of health when he noticed that his urine was blood-tinged. In the following days, he developed urinary incontinence but remained afebrile. He went to see his doctor, and a physical exam revealed suprapubic pain on palpation. Urine cultures were negative, but urine cytology confirmed that the patient was experiencing hematuria. A quantitative BK virus PCR was submitted on the urine specimen and found to be positive with a value of 10,000,000 copies/mL. This strongly suggested BK virus as the cause of this patient’s disease. However, knowing that PCR from urine has a low specificity for diagnosing BK virus-caused kidney disease, which other test could be ordered to make the diagnosis more definitively?
questions.stemHtml: A 55-year-old male kidney-transplant patient was in his usual state of health when he noticed that his urine was blood-tinged. In the following days, he developed urinary incontinence but remained afebrile. He went to see his doctor, and a physical exam revealed suprapubic pain on palpation. Urine cultures were negative, but urine cytology confirmed that the patient was experiencing hematuria. A quantitative BK virus PCR was submitted on the urine specimen and found to be positive with a value of 10,000,000 copies/mL. This strongly suggested BK virus as the cause of this patient’s disease. However, knowing that PCR from urine has a low specificity for diagnosing BK virus-caused kidney disease, which other test could be ordered to make the diagnosis more definitively?

options.label: D
options.text: JC-specific virus PCR from urine to rule out cross-reactivity

questions.solution: Correct Option C - BK virus PCR from plasma: IgG serology would not be helpful because of the high seroprevalence in the general population. Since most adults have been infected with BK virus, serology should not be used for diagnosing acute infection. Serology is a useful tool for assessing seroprevalence in the population and is done more as an investigative tool for epidemiology studies. BK virus urine culture could be done in theory, but the positive urine PCR has already confirmed that BK virus is present in the urine. The reason that urine PCR is not specific is because BK virus can be shed in the urine of asymptomatic immunocompetent and immunocompromised patients alike. Mounting evidence suggests that BK virus can establish latent infection in the kidneys and peripheral blood leukocytes. It is less clear if latent infection occurs in genital tissue, sperm, lung, upper respiratory tract, liver, bone, and brain tissues. Several studies suggest that the sensitivity of plasma PCR for BK virus-caused kidney disease is near 100%, and the specificity is about 88% (higher than the sensitivity of PCR from urine). Incorrect Options: Option A - IgG BK virus serology: JC virus is a closely related polyomavirus that can also be shed in the urine. If proper cross-reactivity studies are not done during development of the BK virus PCR, the presence of JC virus could result in a false-positive PCR. One option not listed is kidney biopsy. This is probably the best method of confirming BK virus disease but is rarely done due to its invasive nature and the fact that a combination of urine and plasma BK virus PCRs offers reasonable sensitivity and specificity. An interesting point about BK virus treatment is that there is some evidence that ciprofloxacin has some activity against BK virus. Option B - BK virus urine culture: Several studies suggest that the sensitivity of plasma PCR for BK virus-caused kidney disease is near 100%, and the specificity is about 88% (higher than the sensitivity of PCR from urine). Option D - JC-specific virus PCR from urine to rule out cross-reactivity: JC can be isolated from plasma rather than from the urine. @Neet_pg_bot

questions.stem: A young male develops intractable pruritus shortly after visiting his family in the remote village. Shortly after, he develops a dry and painful eye. He started on ivermectin. However, his symptoms rapidly deteriorate after the third dose of the medication and subsequent doses. He has a fever, abdominal pain, hypotension, and urticaria. What is the most common explanation for his symptoms?
questions.stemHtml: A young male develops intractable pruritus shortly after visiting his family in the remote village. Shortly after, he develops a dry and painful eye. He started on ivermectin. However, his symptoms rapidly deteriorate after the third dose of the medication and subsequent doses. He has a fever, abdominal pain, hypotension, and urticaria. What is the most common explanation for his symptoms?
questions.solution: Correct Option C - Effect of treatment: This patient exhibits classical symptoms of a Mazzotti reaction, which occurs in reaction to ivermectin. These symptoms resemble classical anaphylaxis, but the severity is related to the load of the parasite and the dose of the medication. This life-threatening complication should be treated promptly with steroids. This drug is known to cause the reaction and should be used cautiously in patients with a high helminth burden. However, praziquantel and albendazole can have similar side effects. Incorrect Options: Option A - Anaphylaxis: Anaphylaxis is a severe and potentially life-threatening allergic reaction that can occur in response to certain medications, foods, insect stings, or other allergens. It is characterized by the sudden onset of symptoms, such as difficulty breathing, swelling of the face and throat, hives or skin rash, and a drop in blood pressure. While anaphylaxis is a possible adverse reaction to medications like ivermectin, it typically occurs shortly after the administration of the medication, not after several doses. In the scenario described, the symptoms are worsening over subsequent doses, which is not consistent with anaphylaxis. Option B - Worsening of infection: While it is possible for an infection to worsen despite treatment, the rapid onset of symptoms like fever, abdominal pain, hypotension, and urticaria after starting ivermectin would not be typical of a worsening infection. Infections usually have a more gradual progression, and the symptoms described in the scenario are more likely to be related to the effect of the treatment rather than a worsening infection. Option D - Septic shock: Septic shock is a life-threatening condition that occurs when an infection leads to a severe systemic inflammatory response, causing a drop in blood pressure and organ dysfunction. While septic shock can result from infections, the symptoms described in the scenario (fever, abdominal pain, hypotension, and urticaria) are more likely to be related to the effect of the treatment (ivermectin) rather than septic shock. Additionally, the rapid deterioration after the third dose of ivermectin is more suggestive of an adverse drug reaction rather than septic shock. @Neet_pg_bot

questions.stem: A 46-year-old male presents with shortness of breath. He has a history of CAD (s/p DES x3 3 years ago) and a distant history of Hodgkin’s lymphoma (s/p chemo with adriamycin [doxorubicin/hydroxydaunorubicin], bleomycin, vinblastine, and dacarbazine). How will his total lung capacity be affected on pulmonary function testing if the patient has developed pulmonary fibrosis?
questions.stemHtml: A 46-year-old male presents with shortness of breath. He has a history of CAD (s/p DES x3 3 years ago) and a distant history of Hodgkin’s lymphoma (s/p chemo with adriamycin [doxorubicin/hydroxydaunorubicin], bleomycin, vinblastine, and dacarbazine). How will his total lung capacity be affected on pulmonary function testing if the patient has developed pulmonary fibrosis?

options.label: D
options.text: Unable to determine from information provided

questions.solution: Correct Option B - Decreased: This patient is likely to have developed pulmonary fibrosis and associated decreased total lung capacity from Bleomycin. Survival of Hodgkin lymphoma (HL) patients has significantly improved in recent times. The current first-line therapy is doxorubicin, bleomycin, vinblastine, and dacarbazine (ABVD) ± irradiation. It is the standard chemotherapy for younger patients. Although it is also used in elderly patients, little is known about toxicity and efficacy. It is known to cause pulmonary toxicity in 10-12% of patients, often many years later and after the primary disease is cured. Strategies to reduce late toxicity and increase survival rate are of obvious interest. ABVD is efficacious in the elderly as well. Due to the higher frequency of pulmonary events in this age group, one might consider removing bleomycin from the regimen or to reduce the dose of bleomycin, as there appears to be no factor that can predict the occurrence of this toxicity. New drugs, such as brentuximab vedotin, have had their efficacies demonstrated in relapsed/refractory HL. The new drugs and new easy geriatric assessment tools, such as G8 which detects frailty, should assist in the better management of these elderly patients. Incorrect Options: Option A - Increased: This option is incorrect because pulmonary fibrosis, especially when caused by medications like bleomycin, leads to a reduction in total lung capacity (TLC), not an increase. Pulmonary fibrosis is characterized by the excessive deposition of fibrous tissue in the lung parenchyma, which stiffens the lungs and reduces their ability to expand during inhalation. As a result, TLC is decreased in restrictive lung diseases like pulmonary fibrosis. Option C - Unchanged: This option is incorrect because pulmonary fibrosis, as mentioned earlier, leads to a decreased total lung capacity (TLC). TLC reflects the total volume of air that the lungs can hold at maximum inhalation. In pulmonary fibrosis, the fibrotic changes in the lung tissue restrict its expansion, resulting in a reduced TLC. Option D - Unable to determine from information provided: This option is incorrect because the provided information strongly suggests the development of pulmonary fibrosis due to the patient's history of Hodgkin's lymphoma and chemotherapy with bleomycin. Bleomycin is known to cause pulmonary toxicity, leading to pulmonary fibrosis in some patients, often years after treatment. Given this history and clinical presentation of shortness of breath, it is reasonable to deduce that the patient's total lung capacity (TLC) will be affected and decreased as a result of the pulmonary fibrosis. The information provided is sufficient to make this determination. @Neet_pg_bot

questions.solution: Correct Option C - Length-time bias: Length-time bias is an error which occurs due to measuring a time interval which is too short, possibly over-representing longer disease processes. This error is especially applicable to lung cancers, which have a wide variability of growth rates. Incorrect Options: Option A - Centripetal bias: Centripetal bias occurs when a study cohort is analyzed through a specific institution or center that may not be representative of the broader population. This can lead to biased results that may not be applicable to the general population. Option B - Lead-time bias: Lead-time bias occurs when a disease is detected earlier through screening or diagnostic tests, but this early detection does not necessarily lead to improved outcomes. This bias can make it appear that a screening test is effective in prolonging survival, when in fact, it may only be detecting the disease earlier without providing any actual benefit in terms of survival. Option D - Reporting bias: Reporting bias refers to the selective inclusion or exclusion of results in a study, which can lead to a distortion of the true relationship between variables. This bias can arise if researchers or journals choose to publish only positive or significant results, while neglecting to publish negative or non-significant findings. @Neet_pg_bot
