questions.stem: What condition does status cataplecticus describe?
questions.stemHtml: What condition does status cataplecticus describe?

options.label: C
options.text: Sustained episodes of cataplexy due to discontinuation of cataplexy-suppressing medication

options.label: D
options.text: Sustained episodes of cataplexy usually due to laughter

questions.answerText: Sustained episodes of cataplexy due to discontinuation of cataplexy-suppressing medication
questions.solution: Correct Option C - Sustained episodes of cataplexy due to discontinuation of cataplexy-suppressing medication: Cataplexy refers to sudden, involuntary muscle atonia in response to laughter, surprise, or other positive and emotionally charged situations; the condition is evident in patients with narcolepsy type 1. Cataplexy may be mild (e.g. slurred speech, a jaw or head drop) to severe (resulting in falls and injuries). The episodes are typically brief, lasting a few seconds to a few minutes. In status cataplecticus (“rebound cataplexy”), episodes of cataplexy recur for hours or days without a refractory period. It is typically due to the abrupt discontinuation of medications that prevent cataplexy, specifically noradrenergic and serotonergic drugs. Status cataplecticus has also been associated with the gradual withdrawal of antidepressants (tricyclics and selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors), and symptoms peak 40-60 days after cessation of the medication. Status cataplecticus may occur with use of prazosin, an α-adrenergic antagonist. Status cataplecticus is not classically associated with the discontinuation of sodium oxybate. Incorrect Options: Option A - Cataplexy with prolonged refractory periods: This option suggests that cataplexy is characterized by prolonged refractory periods. Refractory periods typically refer to the time after a neuron has fired when it's less likely or unable to fire again. However, this doesn't accurately describe cataplexy. Cataplexy is a sudden loss of muscle tone triggered by strong emotions, often laughter or surprise. It is not associated with refractory periods. Option B - Atonic seizures associated with narcolepsy: This option suggests that cataplexy is similar to atonic seizures, which are a type of seizure where there's a sudden loss of muscle tone. While cataplexy and atonic seizures might appear similar on the surface, they have distinct underlying mechanisms. Cataplexy is specifically linked to narcolepsy and is triggered by emotions, whereas atonic seizures are a type of epileptic seizure characterized by sudden loss of muscle strength and consciousness, and they have different triggers and causes. Option D - Sustained episodes of cataplexy usually due to laughter: This option incorrectly states that sustained episodes of cataplexy are usually triggered by laughter. While laughter can indeed trigger cataplexy in some individuals with narcolepsy, it's not the only trigger. Cataplexy can also be triggered by other strong emotions like surprise, excitement, or anger. Additionally, cataplexy episodes are usually brief and involve a sudden loss of muscle tone, rather than being sustained episodes @Neet_pg_bot

questions.stem: A 50-year-old man with a BMI of 31 presents complaining of daytime sleepiness and morning headaches. A sleep-related breathing disorder is suspected. On polysomnography (PSG), the patient has a PaCO2 of >50 mmHg during wakefulness. His obesity and PaCO2 indicate which condition?
questions.stemHtml: A 50-year-old man with a BMI of 31 presents complaining of daytime sleepiness and morning headaches. A sleep-related breathing disorder is suspected. On polysomnography (PSG), the patient has a PaCO2 of &gt;50 mmHg during wakefulness. His obesity and PaCO2 indicate which condition?
questions.solution: Correct Option D - Obesity-related hypoventilation: This patient has a BMI of >30 and a PaCO 2 of >45 mmHg during wakefulness. He most likely has obesity-related hypoventilation. This diagnosis requires a BMI of >30 and an awake PaCO 2 of >45 mmHg (end-tidal PCO 2 , transcutaneous PCO 2 , or arterial PCO 2 may be used to measure this). Incorrect Options: Option A - Obstructive sleep apnea: Obstructive sleep apnea (OSA) often occurs with obesity-related hypoventilation, although elevated PaCO 2 is not part of the diagnostic criteria. A diagnosis of OSA may be made based solely on polysomnographic findings if the patient demonstrates at least 15 respiratory events (obstructive apneas, obstructive hypopneas, or respiratory-related arousals) per hour. In a patient with fewer episodes (5-14 per hour), at least 1 clinical feature must be present from the following: (1) sleepiness; (2) awakening from sleep gasping or choking; (3) witnessed snoring and interruptions in breathing; and (4) a medical condition such as hypertension, type 2 diabetes mellitus, coronary artery disease, history of stroke, cognitive dysfunction, congestive heart failure, or atrial fibrillation. Option B -Central sleep apnea: A diagnosis of central sleep apnea also requires polysomnography (PSG). The patient must demonstrate at least 5 central apneas or hypopneas per hour of sleep. Although a patient with central apnea may have obstructive respiratory events during a study, 50% of all events must be central in nature. Additionally, at least 1 clinical feature is required from the following: (1) sleepiness, (2) poor sleep quality with awakenings/difficulty falling or remaining asleep, (3) snoring, (4) witnessed apneic events, and (5) shortness of breath on awakening. Hypercapnia is not included in these criteria. Option C -Sleep-related hypoxemia: Sleep-related hypoxemia in adults is diagnosed when, on PSG or out-of-center sleep testing (OCST), SpO 2 dips to 88% or below for 5 minutes or longer. A diagnosis of sleep-related hypoxemia is only made in the absence of hypoventilation. A patient who meets criteria for both conditions is given the diagnosis of sleep-related hypoventilation (or in this case, obesity-related hypoventilation). @Neet_pg_bot

questions.solution: Correct Option A - Afatinib Approvals for erlotinib, gefitinib, and afatinib are based on randomized trials that show that each of these eGFR tyrosine kinase inhibitors (TKIs) improve PFS compared to a standard platinum-based 2-drug combination. Incorrect Options: Option B - Combination platinum-based chemotherapy: Chemotherapy showed lower PFS compared to (TKIs). The patient is started on an induction phase of antifungal therapy consisting of amphotericin B and flucytosine for a two-week period. The patient improved over a two-week period and then began to develop inflammation in the CSF, with hypoattenuating CNS lesions on CT imaging. All samples were negative for culture. Which of the following is the most likely cause of the patient’s presentation?

questions.solution: Correct Option B - Immune reconstitution syndrome: Immune reconstitution syndrome (IRS) is an increase in severity of infection-related symptoms following the restoration of the patient’s immune system. Incorrect Options: Option A - Persistent or reactivation of cryptococcus infection: IRS is best distinguished from persistent or reactivation of cryptococcal infection by the fact that active cryptococcal infection would have positive CSF cultures, while IRS is culture negative. The distinction between the two entities is still extremely difficult as similarities such as elevated antigen levels and positive cryptococcal CSF India ink staining are present in both active infection and IRS. Option C - Therapy-related toxicity: The primary toxicity of Amphotericin B is renal dysfunction, while the primary toxicity of flucytosine is bone marrow toxicity. Both of the medications should be frequently monitored during the 2-week induction phase before transitioning to therapy with fluconazole. questions.answerText: Aspirate and send fluid for crystals and MC&S
questions.solution: Correct Option A - Aspirate and send fluid for crystals and MC&S: The most likely diagnosis, in this case, is pseudogout presenting with a pseudorheumatoid pattern of chronic, recurrent swelling affecting primarily large joints. It is often associated with inflammatory symptoms such as stiffness, pyrexia, and malaise. A monoarticular presentation is typical. This option is correct because the patient presents with intermittent pain and swelling in the joints, which could be indicative of crystal-induced arthritis such as gout. Aspirating fluid from the affected joint and sending it for microscopic examination to look for crystals and for microbiological culture and sensitivity (MC&S) to identify any potential infection is a reasonable step in diagnosing the underlying cause of her symptoms. Incorrect Options: Option B - Request anti-CCP: Anti-CCP (anti-cyclic citrullinated peptide) antibodies are primarily associated with rheumatoid arthritis (RA), which is characterized by symmetric polyarthritis affecting smaller joints, morning stiffness, and joint deformities. While RA can cause wrist and hand involvement, this patient's symptoms, along with the presence of Heberden's and Bouchard's nodes, are more suggestive of osteoarthritis. Therefore, anti-CCP testing is not the most appropriate next step. Option C - Request blood cultures: Blood cultures are primarily used to diagnose systemic infections that could lead to septic arthritis. However, the patient's symptoms and clinical findings (Heberden's and Bouchard's nodes) are more consistent with osteoarthritis or possibly crystal-induced arthritis (like gout). Septic arthritis typically presents with more acute and severe joint pain, along with systemic signs of infection. Blood cultures would not be the initial step in this case. Option D - Request serum urate: This option is correct to consider, as elevated serum urate levels are associated with gout. Gout can present with intermittent joint pain and swelling, especially in the joints mentioned in the case. However, the presence of Heberden's and Bouchard's nodes suggests a more typical osteoarthritis presentation. questions.solution: Correct Option C- Left Ventricle: In patients with heart failure , the left ventricle is the most commonly enlarged chamber due to increased workload and pressure overload on the left ventricle. Chronic hypertension and ischemic heart disease are the most common causes of left ventricular dysfunction and dilation, leading to systolic and diastolic dysfunction . The clinical manifestations of left ventricular failure include shortness of breath, fatigue, and signs of fluid overload , such as peripheral edema, ascites, and pulmonary congestion. Echocardiography is the gold standard diagnostic tool to assess left ventricular function and size, and it provides essential information on the ejection fraction , wall thickness, and chamber dimensions. Treatment of left ventricular failure includes optimization of medical therapy , lifestyle modifications , and in severe cases, mechanical circulatory support or heart transplantation. Incorrect Options: Option A- Left atrium: The left atrium may be enlarged in patients with mitral stenosis, mitral regurgitation, or left ventricular failure , but in this patient, the left ventricle is the most likely chamber to be enlarged based on the echocardiographic findings. questions.answerText: Increased preload leads to increased stroke volume
questions.solution: Correct Option A- Increased preload leads to increased stroke volume: Frank-Starling forces refer to the relationship between the volume of blood in the heart at the end of diastole (preload) and the force of contraction during systole. In this patient, the enlarged left ventricle with decreased ejection fraction indicates that the heart is not pumping efficiently. However, the increased preload caused by the enlarged ventricle will lead to an increased force of contraction, which can increase stroke volume and cardiac output to compensate for the decreased ejection fraction. This is the basis of the Frank-Starling mechanism. Incorrect Options: Option B- Decreased afterload leads to increased cardiac output: Afterload refers to the resistance that the heart has to overcome to eject blood from the left ventricle. In this patient, the decreased ejection fraction suggests that the heart is having difficulty overcoming the afterload. Decreasing the afterload may improve cardiac output in some cases, but it is not the primary mechanism at play in this patient's condition. Option C- Increased contractility leads to increased cardiac output: Contractility refers to the force of the heart's contraction independent of changes in preload or afterload. In this patient, the decreased ejection fraction suggests that the heart's contractility is already impaired. Increasing contractility may improve cardiac output, but it is not the primary mechanism at play in this patient's condition. Option D- Decreased preload leads to decreased stroke volume: Decreasing preload would lead to decreased stroke volume , as there would be less blood in the heart to eject during systole. This would further decrease cardiac output in a patient with an already decreased ejection fraction. @Neet_pg_bot

questions.answerText: MVP murmurs are usually louder with inspiration and left lateral decubitus position.
questions.solution: Correct Option C- MVP murmurs are usually louder with inspiration and left lateral decubitus position: MVP is a common cardiac abnormality characterized by the protrusion of one or both leaflets of the mitral valve into the left atrium during systole. The classic murmur of MVP is a mid-systolic click , followed by a late systolic murmur. The intensity of the murmur varies with the position of the patient and the respiratory cycle. During inspiration , the negative intrathoracic pressure increases venous return, thereby increasing left ventricular filling, resulting in increased prolapse of the mitral valve and the intensity of the murmur. The left lateral decubitus position causes the heart to move closer to the chest wall , making it easier to hear the murmur. Therefore, MVP murmurs are usually louder with inspiration and left lateral decubitus position. Incorrect Options: Option A- MVP murmurs are usually louder with standing and valsalva manoeuvre: It is incorrect because standing and valsalva manoeuvre decreases venous return and left ventricular filling, resulting in decreased prolapse of the mitral valve and the intensity of the murmur. questions.stemHtml: Which of the following is the most common congenital heart disease?
questions.solution: Correct Option A-Ventricular septal defect: It is the most common congenital heart disease and the defect commonly occurs in the membranous portion of the septum. The membranous defect occurs on the anterior side of the septal leaflet of the tricuspid valve in the posteroinferior position. The muscular-type septal defect occurs in the apical or mid portion region of the ventricular septum. Patients with small lesions are mostly asymptomatic and at the left lower sternal border a loud harsh holo-systolic murmur often associated with a thrill can be heard during regular physical examination. Congestive heart failure can occur in large VSD due to pulmonary hypertension caused by excessive pulmonary blood flow and can present as dyspnea, failure to grow, and pulmonary infections. Chest radiographs and ECG are usually normal in small VSDs but the presence of right ventricular hypertrophy on ECG is a sign of a large defect and shows that the patient probably has pulmonary hypertension. Echocardiography is done to see the size and position of the defect and cardiomegaly with prominent atrium and ventricles are common x-ray findings in large defects. Incorrect Options: Option B-Atrial septal defect: The atrial septal defect occurs due to failure to develop embryonic septal structures and it can occur in the area of the septum secundum, sinus venous, or septum primum. The atrial septum can be almost completely absent in some rare cases. It most commonly occurs in the region of ostium secundum in the fossa ovalis region. It is mostly asymptomatic failure to thrive in young children and exercise intolerance in older children may be present. Option C-Patent Ductus arteriosus: Failure of ductus arteriosus to close that occurs soon after birth causes shunting of blood from the aorta to the pulmonary artery when pulmonary vascular resistance that is high in fetal life decreases after birth. A machinery-like continuous murmur in the left second intercostal space that may radiate to the left clavicle or sternal border is a common finding. Although small PDAs are asymptomatic, heart failure occurs in large defects and failure to grow can be a common feature in infants. Option D- Coarctation of the aorta: It most commonly occurs in the area of ductus arteriosus origin below the left subclavian artery origin and is more common in males. Temporary relief may be provided by patent ductus arteriosus in the first few days of life as it widens the juxta ductal area. Pain or weakness in the legs after exercise can be complained about by some children. Bounding pulses in the carotids and arm and weak pulses in the lower extremities are common signs. @Neet_pg_bot

questions.stem: A 7-year-old boy is referred to a cardiologist because he was found to have hypertension on a routine physical examination. Palpation of the pulses revealed a radio-femoral delay. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.stemHtml: A 7-year-old boy is referred to a cardiologist because he was found to have hypertension on a routine physical examination. Palpation of the pulses revealed a radio-femoral delay. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.solution: Correct Option B- Coarctation of the aorta: The patient presents with the clinical features of coarctation of aorta. Coarctation of aorta most commonly occurs in the ductus arteriosus origin below the left subclavian artery origin and the patent ductus arteriosus in the first few days of life. Widening the juxta ductal area provides temporary relief. Pulse disparity in the upper and lower extremity is a classic sign of coarctation of the aorta. Simultaneous palpation of radial and femoral pulses should be done to check for the radio-femoral delay. Normally the femoral pulse is palpated just before the radial, and in the coarctation blood supply of descending aorta depends on the collaterals; the femoral pulse is palpated after the radial pulse. Due to narrowing of the aorta, blood pressure is high in the upper body with hypotension and hypoperfusion in the lower body . Subaortic stenosis and mitral valve abnormalities can be associated with it, and these obstructive lesions are called Shone complexes. Pulmonary congestion and cardiomegaly in infants are associated with severe coarctation. In childhood, an enlarged left subclavian artery produces a prominent shadow in the left superior mediastinum. Incorrect Options: Option A- Eisenmenger syndrome: Remodelling of the pulmonary vasculature occurs if the left-to-right shunt is not corrected due to increased pulmonary blood flow, which leads to pulmonary hypertension. Right ventricular hypertrophy occurs with time as compensation, and the shunt becomes right-to-left, resulting in cyanosis, which is called Eisenmenger syndrome. The time of onset depends on the severity of the left-to-right shunt. It does not present with hypertension and radio - femoral delay, hence is an unlikely diagnosis. Option C-Pulmonary valve stenosis: In pulmonary stenosis, deformation of the pulmonary valve cusps results in incomplete valve opening during systole. The central pinhole-like opening is present in severe cases, limiting blood outflow from the right ventricle. Increased systolic ventricular pressure causes right ventricular hypertrophy with time, and signs of right heart failure like exercise intolerance, pulmonary oedema, and hepatomegaly develop in severe stenosis. Auscultation reveals a systolic ejection murmur in the pulmonic area with absence of the pulmonic component of S2. Severe stenosis leads to heart failure. As these features are absent in this patient, it is an unlikely diagnosis. Option D-Ebstein anomaly: Ebstein anomaly occurs when the tricuspid valve is not separated normally from the right ventricular myocardium. All the leaflets apart from the anterior cusp of the valve remain adherent to the right ventricular wall. Right bundle branch block, broad P-waves that may be normal or tall, and normal or prolonged PR-interval are common ECG findings. Box-shaped cardiomegaly is associated with severe cases. Hypertension and radio-femoral delay are not seen in the Ebstein anomaly. @Neet_pg_bot

questions.stem: An obese 68-year-old man has experienced frequent nausea and abdominal pain for the past four months. The pain is in the upper abdomen and gets worse with activity. He has type 2 diabetes, hypertension, and peripheral vascular disease stage 2. For 45 years, he has smoked a single box of cigarettes daily. He consumes one to two beers per day, with more on weekends. Bilaterally, foot pulses are absent. An ECG reveals no unusual patterns. Which of the following is the best next step in the diagnosis process?
questions.stemHtml: An obese 68-year-old man has experienced frequent nausea and abdominal pain for the past four months. The pain is in the upper abdomen and gets worse with activity. He has type 2 diabetes, hypertension, and peripheral vascular disease stage 2. For 45 years, he has smoked a single box of cigarettes daily. He consumes one to two beers per day, with more on weekends. Bilaterally, foot pulses are absent. An ECG reveals no unusual patterns. Which of the following is the best next step in the diagnosis process?

options.label: C
options.text: Abdominal ultrasonography of right upper quadrant

questions.solution: Correct Option A- Cardiac exercise stress test: A cardiac stress test includes a controlled stress simulation to look for stress-induced ischemic changes on cardiac imaging ( echocardiography, myocardial perfusion imaging, cardiac MRI ) or an ECG . Exercise or using the stimulant dobutamine can increase heart rate and contractility, which increases tension or induce the coronary steel phenomenon (using vasodilators such as adenosine, dipyridamole, or regadenoson). A cardiac stress test is usually used to assess blood pressure, heart rate, and electrical conduction of the heart (using an ECG) while the patient exercises under controlled circumstances or after administering a pharmacological agent to mimic cardiac stress. (e.g., adenosine). This patient likely has coronary heart disease, given his prior medical history (stage 2 peripheral arterial disease) and 45 pack-years of smoking. In older adults with diabetes mellitus, coronary heart disease can present as gastrointestinal discomfort rather than retrosternal pain. A resting ECG might not reveal any signs of cardiac ischemia, as it did in this case. However, due to insufficient coronary artery perfusion, this patient will likely have an abnormal outcome on cardiac stress testing (for example, ST depressions). Incorrect Options: Option B- CT scan of the abdomen: A CT image of the abdomen is used to diagnose pancreatitis and intestinal ischemia. These diagnoses are characterized by this patient's recurring abdominal pain and nausea after meals. However, pancreatitis typically produces pain that radiates to the patient's back, which is not seen here. Furthermore, this patient does not exhibit other signs of persistent intestinal ischemia, such as abdominal bloating, food aversion, or weight loss. Furthermore, the worsening of symptoms with physical exercise, as seen in this patient, suggests a different diagnosis. Option C- Abdominal ultrasonography of the right upper quadrant: Ultrasonography of the right upper quadrant of the abdomen is used to test for gallbladder and liver pathologies. However, because this patient's symptoms are linked to exercise, and many risk factors for atherosclerosis are present, another diagnostic study must be conducted. Option D- CT angiography of the abdomen: Intestinal ischemia may be identified using abdominal CT angiography. Patients with chronic intestinal ischemia may experience repeated abdominal pain and nausea after meals. Still, other symptoms like weight loss, food aversion, and stomach bloating would also be anticipated and are not present in this case. Furthermore, a different diagnosis is more likely when symptoms get worse with physical exercise , as experienced in this patient. @Neet_pg_bot

questions.stem: A 58-year-old lady has experienced recurrent chest pain that gets worse with exertion for the past three months. She hasn't experienced any dizziness, palpitations, or loss of breath. She suffers from hyperlipidemia and hypertension. Her current medicines include rosuvastatin, metoprolol, amlodipine, lisinopril, and estrogen replacement therapy. She drinks 4 cups of coffee every day. The findings of routine serum studies reveal no anomalies, and a resting ECG reveals a normal sinus rhythm. In two days, she will undergo a cardiac exercise stress test. Which of the following should you stop taking the day before the procedure?
questions.stemHtml: A 58-year-old lady has experienced recurrent chest pain that gets worse with exertion for the past three months. She hasn't experienced any dizziness, palpitations, or loss of breath. She suffers from hyperlipidemia and hypertension. Her current medicines include rosuvastatin, metoprolol, amlodipine, lisinopril, and estrogen replacement therapy. She drinks 4 cups of coffee every day. The findings of routine serum studies reveal no anomalies, and a resting ECG reveals a normal sinus rhythm. In two days, she will undergo a cardiac exercise stress test. Which of the following should you stop taking the day before the procedure?
questions.solution: Correct Option A- Metoprolol and coffee intake: Beta-blockers (e.g., metoprolol) and calcium channel blockers (CCBs), particularly nondihydropyridine CCBs (e.g., verapamil), can reduce the diagnostic value of cardiac exercise stress testing by attenuating the chronotropic and inotropic effects of exercise. The clinician may decide to withhold these medications previous to testing. Methylxanthines (e.g. theophylline) are competitive adenosine receptor inhibitors that raise the risk of arrhythmias, making it difficult to complete cardiac stress tests or understand the results of those tests. Suppose the patient is unable to reach a desired heart rate with exercise. In that case, the exercise stress test may need to be changed to a pharmacological stress test , so stopping methylxanthines should also be considered. Methylxanthines interact with a pharmacological stress test using vasodilator agents because they reduce coronary vasodilation (e.g., adenosine, dipyridamole). Incorrect Options: Option B- Rosuvastatin and coffee intake: Statins do not affect cardiac stress testing. Option C-Rosuvastatin and hydrochlorothiazide: Cardiovascular stress testing is not affected by statins like rosuvastatin. Before undergoing cardiac stress testing, patients who do not have electrolyte problems can continue taking diuretics (like hydrochlorothiazide ). Option D- Lisinopril and estrogen: ACE inhibitors, such as lisinopril, do not substantially impede cardiac stress testing. The effects of postmenopausal estrogen replacement therapy on the risk of coronary artery disease (CAD) are less obvious than those of estrogen-containing oral contraceptives, which contain high doses of estrogen and are contraindicated in patients with CAD. In any case, there is no advice against delaying estrogen therapy before cardiac stress testing due to the conflicting data on the effects of estrogen on cardiac exercise stress testing. @Neet_pg_bot

questions.stem: Which of the following statements about the membrane potential in neurons is accurate?
questions.stemHtml: Which of the following statements about the membrane potential in neurons is accurate?

options.label: A
options.text: The resting membrane potential is negative because the neuronal plasma membrane is much more permeable to potassium ions relative to other ions.

options.label: B
options.text: The resting membrane potential is negative because the neuronal plasma membrane is much more permeable to sodium ions relative to other ions.

options.label: C
options.text: The resting membrane potential is negative because the neuronal plasma membrane is much less permeable to chloride ions relative to other ions.

options.label: D
options.text: The resting membrane potential is negative because the neuronal plasma membrane is much more permeable to calcium ions relative to other ions.

questions.answerText: The resting membrane potential is negative because the neuronal plasma membrane is much more permeable to potassium ions relative to other ions.
questions.solution: Correct Option A - The resting membrane potential is negative because the neuronal plasma membrane is much more permeable to potassium ions relative to other ions The equilibrium potential of potassium, representing the transmembrane electrical potential at which net flow of potassium ions across the membrane is zero, is around -75 to -80 mV. As noted in the Nernst equation, this value is determined by the concentration of the specific ion inside versus outside the cell and the net charge on each side of the cell membrane. The membrane equilibrium potential is derived from a combination of the equilibrium potentials of the individual ions in combination with the membrane permeability of each ion. The more permeable the membrane is to an individual ion, the more influence that ion will have on the membrane equilibrium potential. Therefore, at rest when the membrane is much more permeable to potassium than any other ion, the membrane equilibrium potential at rest (usually ~ -75 mV) approximates but does not completely reach the equilibrium potential of potassium (~ -75 to -80 mV). By the same rationale, when the axon is depolarized via influx of sodium ions into the cell and the depolarization is large enough to further increase the inward sodium current (positive feedback) via opening of additional voltage gated-sodium channels, the increased permeability of sodium will translate into the membrane potential moving towards the equilibrium potential for sodium (e.g., + 55 mV) until sodium channels close via their inactivation gates and voltage-gated potassium channels open, both resulting in a shift back towards the potassium equilibrium potential (i.e., repolarization phase). In their resting state, most neurons are highly permeable to potassium, moderately permeable to chloride, and minimally permeable to sodium and calcium. Incorrect Options: Option B - The resting membrane potential is negative because the neuronal plasma membrane is much more permeable to sodium ions relative to other ions The statement is not accurate. Neuronal membranes are more permeable to potassium ions, not sodium ions, which is why the resting membrane potential is negative. Option C -The resting membrane potential is negative because the neuronal plasma membrane is much less permeable to chloride ions relative to other ions The statement is not accurate. The resting membrane potential is not primarily influenced by chloride ions' permeability. Option D - The resting membrane potential is negative because the neuronal plasma membrane is much more permeable to calcium ions relative to other ions The statement is not accurate. Neuronal membranes are more permeable to potassium ions, not calcium ions. @Neet_pg_bot

Therefore, at rest when the membrane is much more permeable to potassium than any other ion, the membrane equilibrium potential at rest (usually ~ -75 mV) approximates but does not completely reach the equilibrium potential of potassium (~ -75 to -80 mV). questions.stem: A 32-year-old woman with a history of depression presents to the emergency department with sudden onset of severe headache 24 hours prior to presentation. She has no history of headaches, grades this as the worst headache of her life and says that it was maximal at onset. Over the last 24 hours she has tried Tylenol and Motrin without any relief. The headache has fluctuated in intensity over the last 24 hours and will intermittently return to 10/10 in intensity. At intake she has an elevated blood pressure with borderline tachycardia, is afebrile, and her general and neurologic examinations are normal. Her medications include: citalopram, pseudoephedrine (Sudafed) prn, clonazepam prn, and a multivitamin. A urine drug screen is positive for cocaine and amphetamines. Additional laboratory studies are unremarkable (including a rapid HIV screen and a urine hCG) and a non-contrast head CT is normal. After the uneventful administration of one millilitre of 1% Lidocaine a lumbar puncture is performed, and CSF is obtained on the first pass with a 22 gauge Sprotte needle. The opening pressure is 18 cm H2O, CSF protein is 45 mg/dL, and glucose is 67 mg/dL (serum = 100 mg/dL). Xanthochromia is present in tubes 1 and 4 and there are 1,254 and 4,250 red blood cells, respectively, without nucleated cells. After the patient is admitted her husband shows up panicked and asks about her prognosis for recovery. Which of the following would be the most appropriate response?

After the patient is admitted her husband shows up panicked and asks about her prognosis for recovery. Which of the following would be the most appropriate response?

options.label: A
options.text: She will require ICU admission for at least 14-21 days to monitor for worsening vasospasm.

options.label: B
options.text: Most patients develop strokes or intraparenchymal haemorrhages and unfortunately there is very little that can be done to prevent these from occurring, even with removal of the offending agents.

options.label: C
options.text: Most patients make a full recovery within a few weeks with supportive care alone.

options.label: D
options.text: You have started her on diltiazem and the addition of calcium channel blockers hastens resolution and leads to improved outcomes.

questions.answerText: Most patients make a full recovery within a few weeks with supportive care alone.
questions.solution: Correct Option C - Most patients make a full recovery within a few weeks with supportive care alone The prognosis for this illness is usually excellent. Most patients, even those with SAH, make a complete recovery within days to weeks. More severe cases, in which patients develop ischemic infarcts or intraparenchymal haemorrhages (secondary to vasospasm), have prognoses on par with that associated for patients with other forms of stroke. Death is rare and is usually associated with fulminant generalized vasoconstriction unresponsive to therapy. Patients with aneurysmal SAH that develop vasospasm are often monitored for extended periods in ICU settings given their very high risk for complications and need for ICU level of care. However, the same approach is not indicated in RCVS patients. As per above, there is no evidence to say that use of calcium channel blockers affects outcome. There is no indication for a repeat LP unless clinically indicated for a different reason. However, follow up angiography (usually via non-invasive angiography, e.g., CT or MR angiography) at 4-8 weeks is typically performed to confirm resolution/improvement as reversibility is necessary to make a definite diagnosis of RCVS and persistence of the caliber changes may warrant reconsideration of the diagnosis, particularly if clinical symptoms have not resolved/improved. Incorrect Options: Option A - She will require ICU admission for at least 14-21 days to monitor for worsening vasospasm ICU admission for 14-21 days to monitor for worsening vasospasm is not generally required for all patients with SAH. While vasospasm can be a complication after SAH, not all patients will experience severe vasospasm requiring prolonged ICU admission. Option B - Most patients develop strokes or intraparenchymal haemorrhages and unfortunately there is very little that can be done to prevent these from occurring, even with removal of the offending agents The statement that most patients develop strokes or intraparenchymal hemorrhages and there is little that can be done to prevent these is not accurate. While SAH carries risks of complications, including vasospasm and rebleeding, many patients do recover with appropriate management. Option D - You have started her on diltiazem and the addition of calcium channel blockers hastens resolution and leads to improved outcomes While calcium channel blockers like nimodipine are used to prevent and treat vasospasm after SAH, the presence of blood breakdown products in the CSF (xanthochromia) and the elevated red blood cell count suggest that the primary focus should be on the initial management of the SAH itself. Furthermore, the use of diltiazem is not a common standard of care for SAH. @Neet_pg_bot

The calculated volume of the hematoma is 45 ml (based on the ABC/2 formula). Based on the data provided his ICH score is 3.
The ICH score was designed as a clinical grading tool to estimate which of the following?
questions.solution: Correct Option D - 30-day mortality The ICH score is a clinical grading scale and can be useful in estimating 30-day mortality. The scale ranges from 0-6 with 6 being associated with the highest mortality. One point is assigned for each of the following: Age > 80 years, ICH Volume > 30 ml, associated intraventricular hemorrhage, and infratentorial location. One point is given for a Glasgow Coma Scale (GCS) of 5-12 and two points are given for a GCS of 3-4. Incorrect Options: Option A - 90-day modified Rankin score: The 90-day modified Rankin score assesses a patient's functional outcome after a stroke, including intracerebral hemorrhage. It measures the degree of disability or dependence in daily activities. While the ICH score can help predict mortality, it is not specifically designed to estimate the 90-day modified Rankin score. Option B - Probability of herniation: The probability of herniation is not directly estimated using the ICH score. Herniation is a potentially life-threatening complication that can occur when there is increased intracranial pressure due to factors such as a large intracerebral hemorrhage. However, the ICH score primarily focuses on predicting 30-day mortality. Option C - Risk for hematoma expansion: The risk for hematoma expansion is not directly estimated by the ICH score. questions.stem: A 72-year-old gentleman presents to the emergency department after a 20-minute episode of left sided weakness which was completely resolved prior to arrival. An MRI of the brain demonstrates a punctate area of restricted-diffusion in the right thalamus. Which of the following is the correct diagnosis in this case?
questions.stemHtml:
A 72-year-old gentleman presents to the emergency department after a 20-minute episode of left sided weakness which was completely resolved prior to arrival. An MRI of the brain demonstrates a punctate area of restricted-diffusion in the right thalamus.
Which of the following is the correct diagnosis in this case?
questions.solution: Correct Option C - Ischemic stroke The ‘classic’ definition of transient ischemic attack (TIA) is a sudden, focal neurologic deficit attributed to transient brain or eye ischemia lasting less than 24 hours. Advances in neuroimaging and the early imaging detection of ischemia have helped refine our understanding, and therefore our definition, of TIAs. Indeed, nearly half of patients who present with a classic TIA have MRI evidence of acute infarction on diffusion-weighted imaging. As a result the American Heart Association (AHA) and American Stroke Association ASA, revised the definition of TIA to a transient episode of neurologic dysfunction caused by focal brain, spinal cord, or retinal ischemia, without acute infarction. Here, the patient has complete resolution of symptoms; however there is neuroimaging evidence of infarction making the diagnosis an ischemic stroke. Incorrect Options: Option A - Transient ischemic attack: Transient ischemic attack (TIA) is a brief episode of neurological dysfunction caused by a temporary disruption of blood flow to a specific brain area. TIAs typically last for less than 24 hours and do not cause permanent brain damage. While the patient's symptoms could resemble a TIA, the MRI finding of restricted diffusion indicates that an ischemic event did occur. Option B - Hemorrhagic stroke: Hemorrhagic stroke involves bleeding within or around the brain tissue. The MRI finding of restricted diffusion suggests ischemic rather than hemorrhagic pathology. Option D - Complicated migraine: Complicated migraine is characterized by migraine headache accompanied by neurological symptoms such as visual disturbances (aura) and other focal neurological deficits. However, the MRI finding of a punctate area of restricted diffusion is more consistent with an ischemic event rather than a complicated migraine. @Neet_pg_bot

questions.stem: A 32 year-old woman developed orthostatic headaches, tinnitus and interscapular pain after an afternoon playing on the trampoline with her children. You suspect a spontaneous cerebrospinal fluid leak and are considering performing a radioisotope cisternography as part of her evaluation. Which of the following is true regarding this diagnostic procedure?
questions.stemHtml:
A 32 year-old woman developed orthostatic headaches, tinnitus and interscapular pain after an afternoon playing on the trampoline with her children. You suspect a spontaneous cerebrospinal fluid leak and are considering performing a radioisotope cisternography as part of her evaluation.
Which of the following is true regarding this diagnostic procedure?

options.label: A
options.text: In radioisotope cisternography paradural extravasation of the radioisotope is the direct evidence of spinal CSF leak and is the most common abnormal finding

options.label: B
options.text: In patients with very slow leaks CT-myelography is more likely to show indirect evidence of leak than radioisotope cisternography

options.label: C
options.text: Radioisotope cisternography is most helpful in identifying the site of the leak when its presence has been established by a classical clinical presentation or another diagnostic modality

options.label: D
options.text: When there is spinal leakage of CSF the cephalad migration of the radioisotope slows down which results in reduced or absent radioactivity over the cerebral convexities at 24 hours

questions.answerText: When there is spinal leakage of CSF the cephalad migration of the radioisotope slows down which results in reduced or absent radioactivity over the cerebral convexities at 24 hours
questions.solution: Correct Option D - When there is spinal leakage of CSF the cephalad migration of the radioisotope slows down which results in reduced or absent radioactivity over the cerebral convexities at 24 hours Radioisotope cisternography is a diagnostic procedure used to detect cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) leaks, particularly spontaneous CSF leaks that can lead to orthostatic headaches, tinnitus, and other symptoms. During this procedure, a radioactive tracer is injected into the patient's cerebrospinal fluid. The movement of the tracer is then tracked using imaging techniques to identify the presence and location of CSF leaks. When there is a spinal CSF leak, the radioisotope tracer injected into the CSF will migrate upward in the spinal canal. However, due to the leak, the migration of the tracer towards the head is slowed down or blocked. This leads to reduced or absent radioactivity over the cerebral convexities (the outer surfaces of the brain) at 24 hours after injection. This phenomenon serves as evidence of a CSF leak, supporting the diagnosis. Incorrect Options: Option A - In radioisotope cisternography paradural extravasation of the radioisotope is the direct evidence of spinal CSF leak and is the most common abnormal finding Paradural extravasation of the radioisotope is not the most common abnormal finding in radioisotope cisternography. The slow migration of the tracer as described in the correct answer is a more common and significant finding associated with CSF leaks. Option B - In patients with very slow leaks CT-myelography is more likely to show indirect evidence of leak than radioisotope cisternography In patients with very slow leaks, radioisotope cisternography is more likely to demonstrate the slow migration of the tracer and reduced radioactivity over the cerebral convexities. CT-myelography is not necessarily better for showing indirect evidence of slow leaks; rather, it's a different imaging modality used to visualize the spinal cord and nerves. Option C - Radioisotope cisternography is most helpful in identifying the site of the leak when its presence has been established by a classical clinical presentation or another diagnostic modality Radioisotope cisternography is not primarily used to identify the site of the leak after its presence has been established by clinical presentation or another diagnostic modality. It is used to both confirm the presence of a CSF leak and help locate its site. The slow migration of the tracer helps identify the location of the leak. @Neet_pg_bot

  • Radioisotope cisternography is a diagnostic procedure used to detect cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) leaks, particularly spontaneous CSF leaks that can lead to orthostatic headaches, tinnitus, and other symptoms. During this procedure, a radioactive tracer is injected into the patient's cerebrospinal fluid. The movement of the tracer is then tracked using imaging techniques to identify the presence and location of CSF leaks.
  • When there is a spinal CSF leak, the radioisotope tracer injected into the CSF will migrate upward in the spinal canal. However, due to the leak, the migration of the tracer towards the head is slowed down or blocked. This leads to reduced or absent radioactivity over the cerebral convexities (the outer surfaces of the brain) at 24 hours after injection. This phenomenon serves as evidence of a CSF leak, supporting the diagnosis.

Incorrect Options:

Option A - In radioisotope cisternography paradural extravasation of the radioisotope is the direct evidence of spinal CSF leak and is the most common abnormal finding

Paradural extravasation of the radioisotope is not the most common abnormal finding in radioisotope cisternography. The slow migration of the tracer as described in the correct answer is a more common and significant finding associated with CSF leaks.

Option B - In patients with very slow leaks CT-myelography is more likely to show indirect evidence of leak than radioisotope cisternography

In patients with very slow leaks, radioisotope cisternography is more likely to demonstrate the slow migration of the tracer and reduced radioactivity over the cerebral convexities. CT-myelography is not necessarily better for showing indirect evidence of slow leaks; rather, it's a different imaging modality used to visualize the spinal cord and nerves.

Option C - Radioisotope cisternography is most helpful in identifying the site of the leak when its presence has been established by a classical clinical presentation or another diagnostic modality

Radioisotope cisternography is not primarily used to identify the site of the leak after its presence has been established by clinical presentation or another diagnostic modality. It is used to both confirm the presence of a CSF leak and help locate its site. The slow migration of the tracer helps identify the location of the leak.

Her husband is concerned that she can no longer remember the specific designers of some of her most prized articles and refers to everything as being from "Calvin Klein." This is a deficit in which of the following subtypes of memory?
questions.stemHtml:
A 55-year-old woman is brought to the office by her husband for problems with thinking and memory. One of her long standing hobbies has been fashion. Her husband is concerned that she can no longer remember the specific designers of some of her most prized articles and refers to everything as being from "Calvin Klein."
This is a deficit in which of the following subtypes of memory?
questions.solution: Correct Option B - Semantic memory This is an example of a deficit in semantic memory. Semantic memory refers to acquired knowledge with regard to an individual’s world (i.e., the environment that surrounds them) and the relationship between entities within that world. Unlike episodic memory, which often has a personal basis (one’s experiences make up its content), semantic memory deals with concepts independent of the individual (i.e., more generalized concepts). This category encompasses facts, concepts, objects and their uses, words and their definition. Accordingly, common early manifestations of deficits in semantic memory may be “word finding” difficulties or frank anomia. Semantic paraphasias are common, and low frequency words may be substituted for higher frequency words with categorical overlap. Incorrect Options: Option A - Episodic memory: Episodic memory is the subtype of memory responsible for remembering personal experiences and events, including the context in which they occurred. This type of memory is not primarily related to the woman's inability to recall specific fashion designers. Option C - Working memory: Working memory is the temporary storage and manipulation of information needed for cognitive tasks such as problem-solving and reasoning. The scenario does not describe issues related to working memory deficits. Option D - Procedural memory: Procedural memory involves the memory of how to perform various skills and tasks, often involving motor or cognitive processes. It is not directly related to the woman's difficulty in remembering fashion designers. @Neet_pg_bot

questions.stem: A 65-year-old man with hypertension and diabetes suffers a stroke which leaves him with a residual language deficit. He can follow complex commands without difficulties and reading is normal. His fluency is minimally impaired with frequent paraphasic errors. Naming is largely normal but repetition is poor. What language dysfunction is this most consistent with?
questions.stemHtml:

His fluency is minimally impaired with frequent paraphasic errors. Naming is largely normal but repetition is poor.

questions.solution: Correct Option D - Conduction aphasia: Damage to the dominant cerebral hemisphere can result in several disorders of language. Close examination of the six components of language (fluency, comprehension, repetition, reading, writing and naming) can help distinguish these syndromes. The case describes someone whose main deficit is impaired repetition, frequent paraphasic errors and mildly affected fluency. This is consistent with conduction aphasia which is a rare form of aphasia associated with lesions of the arcuate fasciculus (option d is correct). Incorrect Options: Option A - Broca’s aphasia: Broca's aphasia is characterized by non-fluent speech, effortful production, and limited grammatical structures. Patients with Broca's aphasia often struggle with producing complex sentences and may have difficulty following complex commands. Option B - Wernicke's aphasia: It is characterized by fluent speech with impaired comprehension and meaningful content that doesn't make logical sense (also known as "word salad"). Reading is also often impaired in Wernicke's aphasia. Option C - Transcortical aphasias: It involves damage to brain areas surrounding the core language centers. These aphasias share some characteristics with classic aphasias but often have distinct patterns of language deficits. However, the patient's profile is more consistent with conduction aphasia than a transcortical variant. @Neet_pg_bot

questions.stem: A 62-year old man is brought to the office by his wife for a 6-month history of repetitive movements in his sleep. His wife says that these episodes typically happen later in the night, a few hours before he normally wakes up. He punches at his pillow, move his legs as if he were running or talks. If he wakes up during these events he interacts appropriately and will usually recall a dream that corresponds to what he was doing, like he was being chased or was fighting. Last week, he punched his wife during one of these spells and she now sleeps in the spare bedroom. He has now had approximately 10 of these episodes. He has no other complaints. He denies any trouble falling asleep or staying asleep and denies any sleepiness in the daytime. His wife has not noticed any snoring or gasping. He takes a beta-blocker blocker for hypertension and no other medications. He does not smoke and drinks alcohol rarely. You decide to order an overnight sleep study for further evaluation. What polysomnographic finding would confirm this patient’s probable diagnosis?

questions.answerText: Elevated muscle tone in REM sleep
questions.solution: Correct Option A - Elevated muscle tone in REM sleep: This patient’s clinical presentation is very suggestive of REM sleep behavior disorder (RBD) in which patients do not develop atonia during REM sleep causing them to act out their dreams in a violent fashion, often resulting in injury to themselves or others. The recollection of coherent dream content corresponding to the motor behavior is typical of RBD. RBD typically emerges later in life, after age 50, and has a male predominance. The diagnosis of RBD requires polysomnographic confirmation by demonstration of elevated muscle tone during REM sleep. Incorrect Options: Option B - Short latency to REM sleep : Short latency to REM sleep is not a characteristic finding in REM sleep behavior disorder (RBD). In fact, RBD is associated with a loss of normal REM sleep atonia, not an alteration in REM sleep latency. Option C - Frequent episodes of restriction in airflow associated with oxygen desaturations : Frequent episodes of restriction in airflow associated with oxygen desaturations suggest obstructive sleep apnea, which is not consistent with the patient's presentation of RBD. Option D - Generalized paroxysmal rhythmic activity : Generalized paroxysmal rhythmic activity is not a characteristic finding of RBD. It is more suggestive of a seizure disorder or other abnormal brain activity during sleep. @Neet_pg_bot

questions.stemHtml: Which of the following is true regarding trigeminal neuralgia?

options.label: A
options.text: The pain most often involves the first division of the trigeminal nerve (V1)

options.text: It affects men more than women

options.text: Cutaneous triggers are common and the trigger zone may not coincide with the location of the pain

options.label: D
options.text: Neuroimaging is not helpful in the evaluation of trigeminal neuralgia

questions.answerText: Cutaneous triggers are common and the trigger zone may not coincide with the location of the pain
questions.solution: Correct Option C - Cutaneous triggers are common and the trigger zone may not coincide with the location of the pain: Trigeminal neuralgia (TN) is the most common cranial neuralgia. The pain in TN rarely localizes to the V1 distribution (less than 5 % of cases) and most often involves the second and third distributions of the trigeminal nerve. Painful attacks in TN can occur spontaneously or be triggered by tactile stimulation of specific areas. These are often in the skin around the mouth and the nose and do not necessarily have to fall within the area affected by the pain. Symptomatic trigeminal neuralgia can occur in the setting of a variety of structural lesions including meningiomas, aneurysms and demyelinating lesions. Incorrect Options: Option A - The pain most often involves the first division of the trigeminal nerve (V1) : Trigeminal neuralgia most commonly involves the second (V2) and third (V3) divisions of the trigeminal nerve. Pain involving the first division (V1) is less common. Option B - It affects men more than women : Trigeminal neuralgia is more commonly reported in women than men. Option D - Neuroimaging is not helpful in the evaluation of trigeminal neuralgia : Neuroimaging, such as MRI, can be helpful in the evaluation of trigeminal neuralgia to rule out structural causes that might mimic the condition, such as tumors compressing the trigeminal nerve. It's important to perform neuroimaging to ensure an accurate diagnosis. Option E - Age of onset is typically in the late teens and early twenties: The typical age of onset for trigeminal neuralgia is around 50 to 60 years old. Onset in the late teens and early twenties is less common. @Neet_pg_bot

He is reviewed 2 weeks later in the clinic where you note increased weakness of shoulder muscles particularly shoulder abductors and wasting of the right shoulder musculature compared to the left his range of movement passively is reasonably preserved. Reflexes remain diminished on the right and on detailed neurological examination you notice some patchy areas of sensory loss. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.stemHtml:
A 25-year-old man is seen in the middle of the night with severe right shoulder pain. He describes the pain as 10/10 intensity. He has no significant past medical history but had received an influenza vaccination 3 days prior to the admission. Examination of the shoulder is difficult but limited due to pain, neck movements are normal. Reflexes are present but diminished on the right side. The limb is warm and pulses are palpable. A plain radiograph of the shoulder is normal.
His pain is controlled with a combination of tramadol and non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs and he is discharged home. He is reviewed 2 weeks later in the clinic where you note increased weakness of shoulder muscles particularly shoulder abductors and wasting of the right shoulder musculature compared to the left his range of movement passively is reasonably preserved. Reflexes remain diminished on the right and on detailed neurological examination you notice some patchy areas of sensory loss.
What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.solution: Correct Option D - Neuralgic amyotrophy: Neuralgic amyotrophy or brachial neuritis is a plexopathy that particularly affects the lower motor neurons of the brachial plexus and can be both inherited or idiopathic. The idiopathic form can be triggered by certain events such as trauma, viral or bacterial infection or vaccination. The patient presents as in this case with excruciating shoulder pain with subsequent progressive and often patchy motor and sensory changes. The diagnosis can be confirmed on nerve conduction studies (NCS) and electromyography (EMG) with loss of sensory and motor amplitudes on NCS and denervation on needle EMG. These changes may take a week or more to develop. Treatment of the condition is with adequate analgesia and physical therapy. Incorrect Options: Option A - Acute Poliomyelitis: Acute poliomyelitis is a viral infection that primarily affects the motor neurons in the spinal cord, leading to muscle weakness and paralysis. It is characterized by sudden onset fever, headache, vomiting, and muscle pain followed by asymmetric flaccid paralysis. While this patient does present with muscle weakness and some sensory symptoms, acute poliomyelitis is less likely in this case because: The patient's symptoms started shortly after receiving an influenza vaccination, suggesting a possible immune-mediated or inflammatory response rather than a viral infection. Acute poliomyelitis typically presents with more systemic symptoms like fever, headache, and vomiting, which are not prominent in this patient's presentation. questions.solution: Correct Option D - Macrophage Activation Syndrome: Macrophage Activation Syndrome (MAS) is a severe potentially life-threatening complication of childhood rheumatic conditions . It is most commonly associated with systemic-onset JIA (also known as Still's disease), SLE, Kawasaki disease and may also be seen in Adult-Onset Still's Disease. MAS is one of the hemophagocytic syndromes and can carry a mortality rate of up to 53%. The key clinical features of MAS include fever, hepatosplenomegaly, lymphadenopathy, pancytopenia, deranged ALT, hypertriglyceridemia, disseminated intravascular coagulation, hypofibrinogenaemia, hyperferritinemia. ESR may be paradoxically depressed. Bone marrow aspirate commonly shows hemophagocytosis. Criteria for diagnosis suggested by Ravelli et al are helpful in diagnosing MAS. Additionally, the severe coagulopathy and bruising seen in this case are not typical of mononucleosis. Option B - Haemochromatosis: Haemochromatosis could explain the hyperferritinemia and deranged ALT, but in the absence of liver failure would not explain the coagulopathy. questions.stem: A 74-year-old female presents 40 minutes late to her appointment for evaluation of bilateral hip and shoulder pain for about 6 weeks. She has noticed morning stiffness that lasts until almost noon. In general, she has not been feeling well and has lost 23 kgs in the last 6 weeks. The patient had joint and back aches and pains in the past but nothing as severe as this. She has taken ibuprofen intermittently over the last several weeks without much improvement. She has a history of coronary artery disease and is on aspirin, a statin, and a beta-blocker. She has tolerated a low-dose statin for 15 years. Vitals are as follows: height 5’2”, weight 70 kgs, BP 118/74 mmHg, and HR 62 bpm. Because she is so late for her appointment, a cursory physical exam is performed and shows no weakness or tenderness of the shoulder or hip joints. No rash is noted. Labs are sent, including a CBC, metabolic panel, and ESR. Based on her presentation and probable diagnosis, which additional diagnosis should be considered during this visit?

questions.solution: Correct Option C - Giant cell arteritis: This patient’s symptoms are most consistent with polymyalgia rheumatica. Polymyalgia rheumatica is a chronic, inflammatory disorder of unknown cause. It is not typically seen in people under 50 years of age and has a female predominance. Clinically, the disorder is characterized by pain and long-term morning stiffness affecting the neck, shoulders, hips, upper arms, and thighs. Importantly, 16–21% of patients with polymyalgia rheumatica have giant cell arteritis. Clinically, 40–60% of patients with giant cell arteritis have polymyalgia rheumatica symptoms at diagnosis. Incorrect Options: Option A - Ankylosing spondylitis: Ankylosing spondylitis is a type of inflammatory arthritis that primarily affects the spine and sacroiliac joints. It typically causes pain and stiffness in the lower back and hips, often improving with exercise and worsening with rest. While ankylosing spondylitis could potentially explain some of the patient's symptoms, such as back pain and stiffness, it would not fully account for the bilateral hip pain, shoulder pain, significant weight loss, morning stiffness lasting until noon, and the patient's general malaise. The symptoms and systemic involvement described in the case make ankylosing spondylitis less likely compared to the correct option, giant cell arteritis. Option B - Granulomatosis with polyangiitis: Granulomatosis with polyangiitis (formerly known as Wegener's granulomatosis) is a rare autoimmune disorder that primarily affects the respiratory tract and kidneys. It causes inflammation of blood vessels (vasculitis) that can lead to tissue damage and organ dysfunction. Common symptoms include sinusitis, lung nodules, and kidney problems. While joint pain can occur in granulomatosis with polyangiitis, it is not typically associated with the severe morning stiffness mentioned in the case. Additionally, the patient's symptoms and history do not strongly suggest this diagnosis, making it an incorrect option. Option D - Frozen shoulder: Frozen shoulder, also known as adhesive capsulitis, is a condition characterized by pain and stiffness in the shoulder joint. It occurs when the capsule of connective tissue surrounding the shoulder joint becomes thickened and tight, leading to reduced range of motion. While frozen shoulder can cause significant shoulder pain and stiffness, it does not explain the bilateral hip pain, significant weight loss, morning stiffness lasting until almost noon, and the patient's overall feeling of unwellness. Moreover, frozen shoulders wouldn't account for the patient's history of joint and back aches and pains. Given the broader range of symptoms and systemic involvement, frozen shoulder is an incorrect option. @Neet_pg_bot

questions.stem: The M (microfold) cells are specialized cells found in the Peyer’s patches. Which of the following is a structural feature of these cells?
questions.stemHtml: The M (microfold) cells are specialized cells found in the Peyer’s patches. Which of the following is a structural feature of these cells?

options.label: A
options.text: They have extensive microvilli on their apical surface

options.label: B
options.text: They have a thick mucin overlayer

options.label: C
options.text: They specialize in phagocytosis and endocytosis of luminal antigens

questions.answerText: They specialize in phagocytosis and endocytosis of luminal antigens
questions.solution: Correct Option C - They specialize in phagocytosis and endocytosis of luminal antigens: M cells are transported to the sub-epithelial spaces where they are presented to lymphocytes and other immune cells, initiating an immune response. They do not secrete antibacterial proteins, digestive enzymes, or hormones. They do not contain microvilli and do not absorb luminal nutrients. Incorrect Options: Option A - They have extensive microvilli on their apical surface: Microfold (M) cells do not have extensive microvilli on their apical surface. In fact, M cells have a relatively smooth and flattened appearance on their apical surface, which is in contrast to the extensive microvilli typically found on absorptive cells. This unique structure allows M cells to interact with luminal contents and antigens more directly. Option B - They have a thick mucin overlayer: M cells do not have a thick mucin overlayer. Mucins are glycoproteins that play a role in protecting and lubricating the mucosal surfaces of various tissues, including the gastrointestinal tract. However, M cells do not possess this feature. Instead, they have a specialized structure that facilitates the uptake of antigens from the lumen of the gut. Option D - They contain few lysosomes: M cells actually contain a higher number of lysosomes compared to other cells. Lysosomes are membrane-bound organelles containing enzymes that are involved in cellular digestion and waste processing. M cells contain a higher number of lysosomes because they are actively involved in phagocytosis and endocytosis of luminal antigens, as mentioned in the correct option. These lysosomes play a crucial role in breaking down and processing the internalized antigens. @Neet_pg_bot

questions.stemHtml: Which of the following screening evaluations is recommended for female patients with Lynch syndrome?

options.text: Annual urinalysis examination beginning at age 40, or 5 to 10 years prior to the earliest age of Lynch-associated cancer of any kind in the family

questions.answerText: Endometrial biopsy beginning at age 30, or 5 to 10 years prior to the earliest age of Lynch-associated cancer of any kind in the family
questions.solution: Correct Option D - Endometrial biopsy beginning at age 30, or 5 to 10 years prior to the earliest age of Lynch-associated cancer of any kind in the family: The cancers for which nearly all gastroenterology societies in the United States and abroad recommend routine screening for patients with Lynch syndrome are colorectal and gynecologic cancers. Regarding endometrial cancer screening in asymptomatic women with Lynch syndrome, it is recommended that women undergo annual endometrial sampling, starting at age 30 to 35 or 5 to 10 years prior to the earliest age of Lynch-associated cancer of any kind in the family. Regarding ovarian cancer screening options recommended by experts are an annual pelvic examination, transvaginal ultrasound (TVUS), and cancer antigen 125 (CA 125) every 6 to 12 months, starting at age 30 to 35 or 5 to 10 years prior to the earliest age of first diagnosis of Lynch-associated cancer of any kind in the family. An upper endoscopy is recommended at age 30-35. Annual urinalysis examination is recommended beginning at age 30 to 35 years. Incorrect Options: Option A - Annual urinalysis examination beginning at age 40, or 5 to 10 years prior to the earliest age of Lynch-associated cancer of any kind in the family: This option is incorrect because urinalysis is not a recommended screening evaluation for Lynch syndrome. Lynch syndrome is a hereditary condition that predisposes individuals to certain types of cancers, particularly colorectal and endometrial cancers. Urinalysis is not relevant to Lynch syndrome screening. Option B - Upper endoscopy beginning at age 40, or 5 to 10 years prior to the earliest age of Lynch-associated cancer of any kind in the family: This option is incorrect because upper endoscopy, which involves examining the upper digestive tract, is not a routine screening evaluation for Lynch syndrome. Lynch syndrome primarily involves an increased risk of colorectal and endometrial cancers, so upper endoscopy is not directly related to the syndrome. Option C - Brain MRI beginning at age 40, or 5 to 10 years prior to the earliest age of Lynch-associated cancer of any kind in the family: This option is incorrect because brain MRI is not a standard screening evaluation for Lynch syndrome. Lynch syndrome is mainly associated with colorectal and endometrial cancers, and there is no established connection between Lynch syndrome and brain cancer that would warrant regular brain MRI screenings. @Neet_pg_bot

After initial changes in diet, treatment with loperamide, and bulking agents, she continues to experience episodes of incontinence that cause her embarrassment at work and among friends. Which of the following should you recommend?
questions.stemHtml: A 65-year-old female patient has been diagnosed with passive fecal incontinence due to reduced rectal sensation. After initial changes in diet, treatment with loperamide, and bulking agents, she continues to experience episodes of incontinence that cause her embarrassment at work and among friends. Which of the following should you recommend?
questions.solution: Correct Option B - Biofeedback: After initial supportive measures, including avoidance of trigger foods and improved perianal skin hygiene, a bulking agent such as methylcellulose can be used to supplement the diet for improved stool consistency. Patients with diarrhea should have the underlying cause identified and treated, and loperamide should be initiated to reduce symptoms. After these measures fail, biofeedback can be helpful, particularly in patients who have weakness of the external anal sphincter or nerve injury leading to diminished rectal sensation and an inability to perceive distension. Incorrect Options: Option A - Injection of dextranomer-hyaluronic acid gel: Dextranomer-hyaluronic gel is an injectable agent approved by the FDA in 2011 for treatment of fecal incontinence in patients who have failed conservative measures. It may increase resting anal pressures in patients with passive fecal incontinence. Option C - Anal sphincteroplasty: Anal sphincteroplasty is indicated for patients who fail conservative measures and have an injury to the sphincter muscle identified on anorectal imaging study soon after vaginal delivery. Option D - Sacral nerve stimulation: Sacral nerve stimulation is not a first-line treatment but may be helpful in patients who are not candidates for biofeedback or other therapies. It can be useful in patients with anal sphincter defects and in patients with intact anal sphincter, but the mechanism is unknown. It is effective in patients with fecal incontinence after lower anterior resection and in those with neurological disorders. @Neet_pg_bot

questions.stem: A 62-year-old male is seen for a follow-up evaluation of chronic hepatitis B. He complains of ongoing fatigue, but review of systems is otherwise negative. His medical history is otherwise unremarkable, and he takes no medications. He denies alcohol or tobacco use. On exam, he has no hepatosplenomegaly or signs of portal hypertension. Laboratory studies reveal ALT 24 U/L. Hepatitis serology is as follows: HBsAg + HBeAg + HBeAb + HBV DNA 1,500,000 IU/mL HBV genotype B Ultrasound of the liver is unremarkable. Which of the following is indicated?
questions.stemHtml:
A 62-year-old male is seen for a follow-up evaluation of chronic hepatitis B. He complains of ongoing fatigue, but review of systems is otherwise negative. His medical history is otherwise unremarkable, and he takes no medications. He denies alcohol or tobacco use. On exam, he has no hepatosplenomegaly or signs of portal hypertension. Laboratory studies reveal ALT 24 U/L. Hepatitis serology is as follows:
HBsAg +
HBeAg +
HBeAb +
HBV DNA 1,500,000 IU/mL
HBV genotype B
Ultrasound of the liver is unremarkable. Which of the following is indicated?
questions.solution: Correct Option A - Follow-up laboratory studies in 6 months: The AASLD recommends against antiviral therapy for adults with immune-tolerant chronic hepatitis B infection, which is defined as ALT levels of 35 U/L or less for men and 25 U/L or less for women. According to AASLD guidelines, the immune tolerant phase of chronic hepatitis B infection is characterized by: 1. HBsAg present for 6 months 2. HBeAg positive 3. HBV-DNA levels very high (typically >1 million IU/mL) 4. Normal or minimally elevated ALT and/or AST 5. Liver biopsy or noninvasive test results showing no fibrosis and minimal inflammation Individuals who are in the immune-active phases of infection can be identified by histologic evidence of liver injury, elevated HBV DNA, and elevated ALT. No studies have shown a benefit to antiviral therapy for reduction of hepatocellular carcinoma, cirrhosis, or liver-related death in individuals with immune-tolerant chronic hepatitis B infection. Incorrect Options: Option B - Liver biopsy: Liver biopsy is not required to make a treatment decision in this case. It should be considered in HBeAg-negative patients with elevated HBV DNA >2000 IU/mL who have normal or mildly elevated ALT. Option C - Initial treatment with lamivudine: Treatment is not indicated, and lamivudine monotherapy is rarely recommended for treatment of HBV due to high levels of resistance over time. Option D - Initial treatment with entecavir: Treatment is not indicated in patients in the immune competent phase of chronic hepatitis B infection. @Neet_pg_bot

Correct Option A - Follow-up laboratory studies in 6 months:

The AASLD recommends against antiviral therapy for adults with immune-tolerant chronic hepatitis B infection, which is defined as ALT levels of 35 U/L or less for men and 25 U/L or less for women.

According to AASLD guidelines, the immune tolerant phase of chronic hepatitis B infection is characterized by:

1. HBsAg present for 6 months

2. HBeAg positive

3. HBV-DNA levels very high (typically >1 million IU/mL)

4. Normal or minimally elevated ALT and/or AST

5. Liver biopsy or noninvasive test results showing no fibrosis and minimal inflammation

Individuals who are in the immune-active phases of infection can be identified by histologic evidence of liver injury, elevated HBV DNA, and elevated ALT. No studies have shown a benefit to antiviral therapy for reduction of hepatocellular carcinoma, cirrhosis, or liver-related death in individuals with immune-tolerant chronic hepatitis B infection.

Incorrect Options:

Option B - Liver biopsy: Liver biopsy is not required to make a treatment decision in this case. It should be considered in HBeAg-negative patients with elevated HBV DNA >2000 IU/mL who have normal or mildly elevated ALT.

Option C - Initial treatment with lamivudine: Treatment is not indicated, and lamivudine monotherapy is rarely recommended for treatment of HBV due to high levels of resistance over time.

Option D - Initial treatment with entecavir: Treatment is not indicated in patients in the immune competent phase of chronic hepatitis B infection.
