questions.stem: In your clinic, you care for a 43-year-old male and his 39-year-old sister, both of whom have cirrhosis due to autoimmune hepatitis , however, the brother had a variceal bleed. She presented with elevated transaminases and was subsequently found to have autoimmune hepatitis. At present, both have AST and ALT levels that are less than 40 U/L. She has had several relapses of her disease, while his autoimmune hepatitis has been largely quiescent. He has had cirrhosis for 9 years, while she only developed cirrhosis 3 years ago. Which of the following best describes these patients' relative risk for hepatocellular carcinoma?
questions.stemHtml: In your clinic, you care for a 43-year-old male and his 39-year-old sister, both of whom have cirrhosis due to autoimmune hepatitis , however, the brother had a variceal bleed. She presented with elevated transaminases and was subsequently found to have autoimmune hepatitis. At present, both have AST and ALT levels that are less than 40 U/L. She has had several relapses of her disease, while his autoimmune hepatitis has been largely quiescent. He has had cirrhosis for 9 years, while she only developed cirrhosis 3 years ago. Which of the following best describes these patients' relative risk for hepatocellular carcinoma?

options.label: A
options.text: He has a higher risk for the development of hepatocellular carcinoma than she does because he presented with a variceal bleed.

options.label: B
options.text: She has a higher risk for the development of hepatocellular carcinoma than he does because she had relapses requiring increased immunosuppression.

options.label: C
options.text: Their duration of disease does not impact their risk for HCC.

options.label: D
options.text: The annual incidence rate of HCC in autoimmune hepatitis is 1.1%, surveillance is not recommended for either patient.

questions.answerText: He has a higher risk for the development of hepatocellular carcinoma than she does because he presented with a variceal bleed.
questions.solution: Correct Option A - He has a higher risk for the development of hepatocellular carcinoma than she does because he is presented with a variceal bleed: Variceal bleed at presentation with autoimmune hepatitis is considered to be a cirrhosis equivalent and a risk factor for the development of HCC. Patients with autoimmune hepatitis and cirrhosis present with HCC, on average, about 10 years from the time they are found to be cirrhotic. Thus, their duration of cirrhosis impacts their risk for HCC. Treatment regimen for HCC, response to therapy, and occurrence of relapses do not impact the risk for HCC. Finally, although currently the incidence of HCC is estimated to be 1.1%, this value is extrapolated from the HCV population. Thus, the true incidence of HCC in autoimmune hepatitis is suspected to be 1.5% or higher. AASLD recommends surveillance in all patients with cirrhosis secondary to autoimmune hepatitis. Gender does not impact the risk for HCC in autoimmune hepatitis. Incorrect Options: Option B - She has a higher risk for the development of hepatocellular carcinoma than he does because she had relapses requiring increased immunosuppression: While relapses requiring increased immunosuppression may indicate a more active autoimmune hepatitis, it's the presence of cirrhosis that is a stronger risk factor for the development of hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC). Cirrhosis is a significant predisposing factor for HCC, and it's the duration of cirrhosis that tends to influence the risk more than the severity of autoimmune hepatitis or its relapses. Option C - Their duration of disease does not impact their risk for HCC: The duration of cirrhosis does play a role in influencing the risk of hepatocellular carcinoma. Longer durations of cirrhosis are associated with a higher risk of HCC development. Therefore, the difference in the duration of cirrhosis between the brother (9 years) and the sister (3 years) could potentially impact their relative risk for HCC. Option D - The annual incidence rate of HCC in autoimmune hepatitis is 1.1%, surveillance is not recommended for either patient: While the annual incidence rate of HCC in autoimmune hepatitis might be relatively low, patients with cirrhosis, regardless of the underlying cause, are generally recommended to undergo surveillance for HCC. Cirrhosis is a known risk factor for HCC, and regular surveillance, such as ultrasound and alpha-fetoprotein (AFP) testing, is important for early detection of any suspicious lesions. Therefore, surveillance should be considered for both patients due to the presence of cirrhosis. @Neet_pg_bot

MRI/MRCP reveals a stricture in the proximal pancreatic duct with dilatation beyond the stricture. No mass is seen. Which of the following is appropriate for the evaluation and management of this patient?

questions.solution: Correct Option D - Order endoscopic ultrasound: This patient smokes, which is the most significant environmental risk factor for pancreatic cancer. To determine the cause of the stricture, endoscopic ultrasound should be performed with consideration of fine-needle aspiration. Endoscopic ultrasound is the best test for evaluation of the parenchyma and duct system, making it the best choice for further evaluation of this patient. Incorrect Options: Option A - Repeat MRI/MRCP in 6-12 months: Pancreatic cancer is often unresectable at diagnosis, so in this case the diagnosis should be established quickly to determine whether she has a malignancy that is potentially resectable. Option B - Begin a trial of prednisone for autoimmune pancreatitis: Autoimmune pancreatitis is a possibility, but the diagnosis must be clear before proceeding with treatment. Since the consequences of failing to diagnose a potentially resectable malignancy are clearly grave, the best option is endoscopic ultrasound. Option C - Perform octreotide scan: Octreoscan refers to an Indium-111 pentetreotide scan used to detect carcinoid tumors and their metastases. It is not useful for the diagnosis of pancreatic cancer. @Neet_pg_bot

The pain occurs intermittently in the right upper quadrant, lasts for an hour, and then subsides slowly over the next few hours. She had a cholecystectomy 2 years ago for this type of pain, with minimal improvement. Her LFTs taken at the time of pain were also normal. Her ultrasound shows a dilated CBD to 11 mm. Her CECT abdomen and UGI scopy were normal. The patient is referred for ERCP and manometry. An initial Cholangiogram reveals biliary ductal dilation to 12 mm with no stones. A biliary manometry is performed next. Which of the following Manometric findings predict pain improvement after biliary sphincterotomy?

options.label: B
options.text: Mean basal sphincter pressure >40 mm Hg

questions.answerText: Mean basal sphincter pressure >40 mm Hg
questions.solution: Correct Option B - Mean basal sphincter pressure >40 mm Hg: The clinical presentation is consistent with type 2 SOD dysfunction (biliary-type pain with either elevated liver enzymes or biliary ductal dilation >10 mm). An elevated mean basal sphincter pressure >40 mm Hg is abnormal and was shown to predict improvement in symptoms after sphincterotomy compared to sham procedure. Incorrect Options: Option A - Increased sphincter phasic contractions (>7/min): Increased sphincter phasic contraction, retrograde contractions, and a paradoxical response to cholecystokinin (CCK) are classified as sphincter “dyskinesia” but do not predict symptom improvement after sphincterotomy. Peak sphincter pressure is measured during manometry but is not useful clinically. Option C - Peak sphincter pressure >200 mm Hg: While increased peak sphincter pressure may be associated with sphincter of Oddi dysfunction, it is not a specific predictor of pain improvement after biliary sphincterotomy. Mean basal sphincter pressure is a more relevant parameter in this context. Option D - Increased sphincter retrograde contractions (>50%): Retrograde contractions refer to the backward flow of bile into the biliary duct. Although this finding can be observed in the sphincter of Oddi dysfunction, it is not a specific predictor of pain improvement after biliary sphincterotomy. Mean basal sphincter pressure is a more reliable indicator. @Neet_pg_bot

questions.stem: A 37-year-old female patient with longstanding Crohn’s disease presents with perianal pain and discharge. She has multiple perianal fistulae. Which of the following statements about the management of perianal fistulas in Crohn’s disease is true?
questions.stemHtml: A 37-year-old female patient with longstanding Crohn’s disease presents with perianal pain and discharge. She has multiple perianal fistulae. Which of the following statements about the management of perianal fistulas in Crohn’s disease is true?

options.label: A
options.text: Approximately 90% of perianal fistulas will heal without any treatment.

options.label: B
options.text: Infliximab cannot be used to induce and maintain remission in patients with fistulizing Crohn’s disease.

options.label: C
options.text: Infliximab is immunosuppressive so it is contraindicated in the management of fistulizing Crohn’s disease due to a possible contribution to fistula-associated abscesses.

options.label: D
options.text: Patients who received metronidazole alone for treatment of fistulizing Crohn’s disease had high recurrence rates after discontinuation of therapy.

questions.answerText: Patients who received metronidazole alone for treatment of fistulizing Crohn’s disease had high recurrence rates after discontinuation of therapy.
questions.solution: Correct Option D - Patients who received metronidazole alone for treatment of fistulizing Crohn’s disease had high recurrence rates after discontinuation of therapy: While several agents (including ciprofloxacin, metronidazole, 6-MP, azathioprine, and infliximab) have been effective in the treatment of fistulizing Crohn’s disease (mainly perianal and enterocutaneous fistulas), infliximab therapy had the highest rate of complete fistula closure. When used alone, 46% of patients have a complete response, and 36% have a persistent response at 54 weeks. When used in combination with thiopurines, 75% of patients had complete fistula closure that persisted for at least 6 months. Abscess formation can arise from the closure of the external drainage site prior to closure of the opening from the GI tract. It is suggested that a noncutting seton should be used to reduce the risk of abscess formation in this population by maintaining external drainage until a response to medical therapy is noted. Over 50% of patients treated with metronidazole alone were noted to have complete healing of their perianal disease, but nearly 80% had a recurrence within 4 months of discontinuation of the antibiotic. Incorrect Options: Option A - Approximately 90% of perianal fistulas will heal without any treatment: Perianal fistulas in Crohn's disease can be challenging to manage, and many cases require medical or surgical intervention. Not all perianal fistulas will heal without treatment, especially in the context of Crohn's disease. Option B - Infliximab cannot be used to induce and maintain remission in patients with fistulizing Crohn’s disease: Infliximab is a type of biologic therapy that has been shown to be effective in inducing and maintaining remission in patients with fistulizing Crohn's disease. It is used to target the inflammation that contributes to the formation and persistence of perianal fistulas. Option C - Infliximab is immunosuppressive so it is contraindicated in the management of fistulizing Crohn’s disease due to a possible contribution to fistula-associated abscesses: This statement is not accurate. While infliximab is an immunosuppressive medication, it is commonly used in the management of fistulizing Crohn's disease to reduce inflammation and promote healing of fistulas. It helps control the underlying inflammatory process that contributes to the formation and persistence of fistulas. @Neet_pg_bot

questions.stem: A 73-year-old woman is admitted for evaluation of acute-onset severe epigastric pain followed by vomiting and rapid and forceful defecation. Her medical history is significant for osteoarthritis. She has a temperature of 100.5° Fahrenheit, heart rate of 120 beats per minute, respiratory rate of 20 breaths per minute, and blood pressure of 100/60 mm Hg. Abdominal examination reveals minimal tenderness to palpation and no rebound tenderness or guarding. She has an irregularly irregular heartbeat with a low-pitched diastolic rumble on cardiac auscultation. Which of the following is most likely to be diagnosed?
questions.stemHtml: A 73-year-old woman is admitted for evaluation of acute-onset severe epigastric pain followed by vomiting and rapid and forceful defecation. Her medical history is significant for osteoarthritis. She has a temperature of 100.5° Fahrenheit, heart rate of 120 beats per minute, respiratory rate of 20 breaths per minute, and blood pressure of 100/60 mm Hg. Abdominal examination reveals minimal tenderness to palpation and no rebound tenderness or guarding. She has an irregularly irregular heartbeat with a low-pitched diastolic rumble on cardiac auscultation. Which of the following is most likely to be diagnosed?

options.label: B
options.text: Venous thrombosis of the mesenteric plexus

questions.solution: Correct Option A - Acute mesenteric arterial embolism: The patient’s history and findings are suggestive of acute mesenteric ischemia or acute embolic occlusion that has resulted in interruption of the intestinal blood supply. This most commonly occurs in the superior mesenteric artery and can be related to mesenteric arterial embolism of mesenteric arterial thrombosis. In this patient, an embolic event is the most likely culprit. This patient has a murmur consistent with mitral stenosis, the first presentation of which may be an embolic event, usually involving the cerebrovascular system. Patients with acute mesenteric arterial embolism typically present with a “bowel attack” since an embolic occlusion does not allow the development of collateral circulation. An abrupt cutoff without visualization of distal vessels on angiography is diagnostic of acute embolic occlusion. Incorrect Options: Option B - Venous thrombosis of the mesenteric plexus: Acute mesenteric ischemia can be classified into arterial disease or venous disease. Acute mesenteric ischemia as a result of venous occlusive disease usually refers to mesenteric venous thrombosis. Acute and subacute symptoms are less dramatic than those seen with arterial mesenteric ischemic disorders. Patients are typically younger and have risk factors for hypercoagulability. Prior to the development of acute or subacute abdominal pain, patients may have experienced several weeks of worsening discomfort. Option C - Acute mesenteric arterial thrombosis: The patient has no evidence of cardiovascular risk factors that would suggest possible mesenteric atherosclerosis. Option D - Bezoar: Acute onset of severe pain that is out of proportion to examination findings should suggest acute mesenteric ischemia. @Neet_pg_bot

questions.answerText: Helicobacter pylori infection is a risk factor for both mucosa-associated lymphoid tissue lymphoma and gastric adenocarcinoma.
questions.solution: Correct Option D - Helicobacter pylori infection is a risk factor for both mucosa-associated lymphoid tissue lymphoma and gastric adenocarcinoma: H. pylori is among the most common causes of peptic ulcer disease, in addition to the use of NSAIDs. Treatment of H. pylori in a patient with MALT results in regression of MALT in 80% of affected patients. Incorrect Options: Option A - They have an increased risk of esophageal cancer: This statement is not accurate. Option C - H. pylori infection leads to hyperproliferation of parietal cells: Inflammation caused by H. pylori leads to inhibition of parietal cell secretion and may lead to a loss of parietal cells. @Neet_pg_bot

questions.stemHtml: Which of the following patients has the highest likelihood of developing alloimmunization to platelet transfusion resulting in transfusion refractoriness?

options.label: A

options.label: B
options.text: 52 year old G0P0 female with a random platelet donor

questions.answerText: 52 year old G4P4 female with her son as the platelet donor
questions.solution: Correct Option C - 52 year old G4P4 female with her son as the platelet donor: Generally, multiparous women are more likely than men or nulliparous women to develop alloimmunization to platelets. Furthermore, receiving a transfusion with her son as the donor puts her at an even higher risk, as she may have developed antibodies to the child's father's HLA antigens during her pregnancy. Most cases (~2/3) of platelet refractoriness are NOT due to alloimmunization. However, in cases that are, most are due to antibodies that are created in response to HLA class I antigens on leukocytes or platelets. These antibodies can exist in multiparous women due to maternal-fetal HLA incompatibility during pregnancy. Fetal HLA class I antigens inherited from the father are recognized by the mother as foreign. Multiple pregnancies will put the patient at a higher risk of developing such antibodies. Furthermore, receiving a transfusion with her son as the donor greatly increases the risk of re-presenting HLA class I antigens to antibodies which she has developed.Platelet alloimmunization can also occur in patients who have received multiple transfusions or due to antibodies to platelet specific antigens (human platelet antigens). Incorrect Options: Option A - 52-year-old G0P0 female with her husband as the platelet donor: Alloimmunization to platelet transfusion is more common in multiparous women, as they are exposed to foreign HLA antigens during pregnancy. In this case, the patient has not been pregnant before (G0P0), which lowers her likelihood of developing alloantibodies. Additionally, her husband's HLA antigens are less likely to trigger an immune response compared to antigens from her own offspring. Option B - 52-year-old G0P0 female with a random platelet donor: This patient is also a nulliparous woman (G0P0), reducing her risk of developing alloimmunization to platelet transfusion. questions.stem: Which of the following is a regulatory protein that promotes cell survival by inhibiting apoptosis?
questions.stemHtml: Which of the following is a regulatory protein that promotes cell survival by inhibiting apoptosis?
questions.solution: Correct Option C-Bcl-2: Bcl-2, also known as B-cell lymphoma 2, is an anti-apoptotic regulatory protein that plays a crucial role in promoting cell survival by inhibiting apoptosis. It is a member of the Bcl-2 family of proteins, which regulate the intrinsic or mitochondrial pathway of apoptosis. Bcl-2 is located in the outer mitochondrial membrane and functions to prevent the release of cytochrome c and other pro-apoptotic factors from the mitochondria, thus blocking the activation of the apoptosis cascade. By inhibiting the pro-apoptotic proteins such as BAX and BAK, Bcl-2 helps to maintain the integrity of the mitochondrial membrane and prevent cell death, promoting cell survival. Incorrect Options: Option A- BAX : BAX is a pro-apoptotic protein belonging to the Bcl-2 family. It promotes apoptosis by forming channels in the mitochondrial membrane, leading to the release of cytochrome c and initiating the apoptosis cascade. BAX acts opposite to Bcl-2 and promotes cell death. Option B- BAK : Like BAX, BAK is also a pro-apoptotic member of the Bcl-2 family. It is involved in the permeabilization of the mitochondrial membrane and the release of cytochrome c, triggering apoptosis. BAK works similarly to BAX and promotes cell death. Option D- BAD : BAD is another pro-apoptotic protein belonging to the Bcl-2 family. It acts by binding and inhibiting anti-apoptotic proteins like Bcl-2 and Bcl-XL. Inhibition of these anti-apoptotic proteins can lead to the activation of pro-apoptotic proteins like BAX and BAK, promoting apoptosis. So, BAD is involved in promoting cell death rather than inhibiting it. @Neet_pg_bot

questions.answerText: No difference in resource usage and improved quality of life
questions.solution: Correct Option D - No difference in resource usage and improved quality of life: Project ENABLE II, Bakitas et al. JAMA 2009, looked to determine the effect of a nursing-led intervention on quality of life (QOL), symptom intensity, mood, and resource use in patients with advanced cancer. 322 patients were randomized to a nursing-led, multi-component, psycho-educational intervention or usual care. The effect on quality of life, symptom intensity, mood, and resource use was measured. The intervention consisted of structured interviews and problem solving sessions with at least monthly telephone follow-up sessions until the participant died or the study ended. There were no statistically significant differences in baseline QOL, symptom intensity or depressed mood between the two groups. An improvement in quality of life, symptom intensity and depressed mood was seen in the intervention group. The estimated treatment effects (intervention minus usual care) for all participants were: Quality of life [mean (SE)]: 4.6 (2), p=.02 Symptom Intensity: -27.8 (15), p=.06 Depressed Mood: -1.8 (0.81), p=.02 No differences between the intervention and usual care group were seen in resource use as determined by the number of days in the hospital, number of days in the ICU or number of visits to the emergency department Incorrect Options: Option A - Less resource usage and no difference in quality of life: This option implies that patients who enroll in the palliative care intervention program would use fewer resources, such as healthcare services, but there would be no difference in their quality of life compared to those who do not enroll. This option is incorrect because it doesn't align with the general understanding that palliative care interventions often involve addressing both the physical symptoms and emotional needs of patients to improve their overall quality of life. Option B - No difference in resource usage and no difference in quality of life: This option suggests that enrolling in the palliative care intervention program would result in no differences both in terms of resource usage and quality of life when compared to patients who do not enroll. This is incorrect because palliative care is specifically designed to enhance the quality of life for patients with serious illnesses while also managing their symptoms, which can indirectly impact resource utilization. Option C - Less resource usage and improved quality of life: This option proposes that patients who enroll in the palliative care intervention program would use fewer resources and also experience an improved quality of life. Which of the following patients has the highest likelihood of achieving a cure after undergoing salvage radiation therapy to the prostate bed?
questions.stemHtml: A 68-year-old male, post radical prostatectomy 5 years ago, on follow-up, recently experienced biochemical failure, and he seeks your advice for recommendations regarding the next best step in his treatment course. Which of the following patients has the highest likelihood of achieving a cure after undergoing salvage radiation therapy to the prostate bed?

options.label: A
options.text: Pre-radiation PSA of 0.4 ng/ml, Gleason 3+4=7, Surgical margins positive, PSA doubling time 12 months

options.label: B
options.text: Pre-radiation PSA of 2.3 ng/ml, Gleason 3+4=7, Surgical margins negative, PSA doubling time 8 months

options.label: C
options.text: Pre-radiation PSA of 0.6 ng/ml, Gleason 3+4=7, Surgical margins positive, PSA doubling time 7 months

questions.solution: Correct Option A - Pre-radiation PSA of 0.4 ng/ml, Gleason 3+4=7, Surgical margins positive, PSA doubling time 12 months A retrospective, multi-institutional review (Stephenson et al, J Clin Oncol 2007) developed a nomogram to predict the probability of prostate cancer control at 6-years following salvage radiation therapy (SRT) for PSA-defined recurrence. Overall, 1,603 consecutive patients from 17 North American tertiary referral centers who received SRT after radical prostatectomy for PSA recurrence between 1987 and 2005 were included in the analysis. Prior to SRT, all patients had a PSA level of 0.2 ng/mL or higher at least 6 weeks after radical prostatectomy followed by another higher value, or a single PSA of 0.5 ng/mL or higher. The authors determined that lower pretreatment PSA, lower Gleason score, positive surgical margins, and longer PSA doubling time were prognostic factors that gave the highest probability of prostate cancer control at 6-years following SRT. The authors noted that a PSA doubling time ≥ 10 months was more favorable. Thus, Choice A gives the best probability of prostate cancer cure. This patient has the lowest pretreatment PSA, a low Gleason Score, had positive margins, and a PSA doubling time ≥ 10 months. Please note that positive margin(s) is a favorable prognostic factor as it suggests a higher likelihood that the PSA recurrence is due to disease that is in the prostate bed, and not from a distant metastasis. However, this will not always be true and these patients may still have distant metastases. Incorrect Options: Option B - Pre-radiation PSA of 2.3 ng/ml, Gleason 3+4=7, Surgical margins negative, PSA doubling time 8 months. The higher pre-radiation PSA suggests a greater amount of cancer activity compared to option A. Negative surgical margins indicate that the cancer was completely removed during the surgery. PSA doubling time of 8 months suggests faster growth compared to option A. While this patient's cancer was completely removed, the higher PSA and faster doubling time indicate a higher likelihood of residual or recurrent disease, making the chances of cure after salvage radiation therapy potentially lower compared to option A. Option C - Pre-radiation PSA of 0.6 ng/ml, Gleason 3+4=7, Surgical margins positive, PSA doubling time 7 months. Similar to option A, this patient has a low pre-radiation PSA level, indicating localized disease. Positive surgical margins indicate a higher risk of residual cancer in the area. PSA doubling time of 7 months suggests relatively fast growth compared to options A and B. The faster PSA doubling time reduces the chances of cure compared to option A. Option D - Pre-radiation PSA of 0.8 ng/ml, Gleason 3+4=7, Surgical margins negative, PSA doubling time 11 months. This patient has a relatively low pre-radiation PSA level, indicating localized disease. Negative surgical margins suggest that the cancer was completely removed. PSA doubling time of 11 months is slower compared to option C but faster than option A. This patient's likelihood of cure after salvage radiation therapy might be lower than option A due to the higher PSA doubling time despite the negative surgical margins. @Neet_pg_bot

questions.stem: Prior to the early 1990s, the standard of care for locally advanced laryngeal cancer was surgery (total laryngectomy) followed by postoperative radiation therapy. A pivotal clinical trial changed the standard of care, to definitive chemoradiation, this trial is known as the VA Larynx trial and was reported by Wolf et al. NEJM 1991. What was the trial design of this pivotal clinical trial?
questions.stemHtml: Prior to the early 1990s, the standard of care for locally advanced laryngeal cancer was surgery (total laryngectomy) followed by postoperative radiation therapy. A pivotal clinical trial changed the standard of care, to definitive chemoradiation, this trial is known as the VA Larynx trial and was reported by Wolf et al. NEJM 1991. What was the trial design of this pivotal clinical trial?

options.label: A
options.text: Induction chemotherapy (cisplatin+5-FU) followed by RT if CR/PR versus surgery followed by postoperative radiation

options.label: B
options.text: Concurrent chemoradiation (cisplatin) versus surgery followed by postoperative radiation

options.label: C
options.text: Concurrent chemoradiation (cisplatin) versus induction chemotherapy (cisplatin/5-FU) followed by radiation versus radiation alone (three arms)

options.label: D
options.text: Concurrent chemoradiation (cisplatin/5-FU) versus radiation alone for resectable head and neck squamous cell carcinoma

questions.answerText: Induction chemotherapy (cisplatin+5-FU) followed by RT if CR/PR versus surgery followed by postoperative radiation
questions.solution: Correct Option A - Induction chemotherapy (cisplatin+5-FU) followed by RT if CR/PR versus surgery followed by postoperative radiation The VA larynx Trial (Wolf et al. NEJM 1991) was a practice changing phase III randomized controlled trial. Patients with stage III/IV carcinoma of the larynx were randomized to either: Surgery (total laryngectomy) followed by postoperative radiation therapy (S+RT). Note: this was standard of care at the time of the trial. Induction chemotherapy (Cisplatin and 5-FU, 2 cycles). Patients were then re-evaluated. Patients with at least a partial response received a third cycle of chemotherapy(Cisplatin and 5-FU) followed by radiation therapy (CT+RT). If following radiation therapy they had a complete response, they received no further therapy and proceeded with follow-up. While those patients with partial response after radiation proceeded to salvage surgery (total laryngectomy). If following induction chemotherapy patients had less than a partial response they proceeded to surgery (total laryngectomy) followed by postoperative radiation therapy. The results of the study with a median follow-up of 33 months: 2-year overall survival: 68% S+RT vs. 68% CT+RT p=0.98 2-year disease free survival: "Shorter in the chemotherapy groups, but not statistically significant" (Figure 2 in manuscript) Distant metastatic disease: 17% S+RT vs. 11% CT+RT p=0.04 At four years follow-up: Larynx preserved: 12% S+RT vs. 62% CT+RT (12% of patients had a partial laryngectomy) Total laryngectomy: 88% S+RT vs. 38% CT+RT Patients alive: 52% S+RT vs. 48% CT+RT Patients alive with larynx: 5% S+RT vs. 31% CT+RT T4 tumors also did worse than <T4 tumors. The salvage laryngectomy rate was 56% in T4 tumors vs. 29% in <T4 tumors p=0.001. Incorrect Options: Option B - Concurrent chemoradiation (cisplatin) versus surgery followed by postoperative radiation: This option does not match the design of the VA Larynx trial. The trial didn't compare surgery directly to concurrent chemoradiation with cisplatin. It instead focused on induction chemotherapy followed by radiation versus surgery followed by postoperative radiation. Option C - Concurrent chemoradiation (cisplatin) versus induction chemotherapy (cisplatin/5-FU) followed by radiation versus radiation alone (three arms): This option also does not accurately represent the trial design. The VA Larynx trial had a two-arm design, comparing induction chemotherapy followed by radiation against surgery followed by postoperative radiation. It didn't involve a three-arm comparison that includes concurrent chemoradiation with cisplatin alone and radiation alone. Option D - Concurrent chemoradiation (cisplatin/5-FU) versus radiation alone for resectable head and neck squamous cell carcinoma: This option is not aligned with the trial being discussed. The VA Larynx trial primarily focused on locally advanced laryngeal cancer, and the comparison was between induction chemotherapy followed by radiation and surgery followed by postoperative radiation. It did not include a comparison of concurrent chemoradiation (cisplatin/5-FU) versus radiation alone for resectable head and neck squamous cell carcinoma. @Neet_pg_bot
questions.solutionHtml:
Correct Option A - Induction chemotherapy (cisplatin+5-FU) followed by RT if CR/PR versus surgery followed by postoperative radiation

The VA larynx Trial (Wolf et al. NEJM 1991) was a practice changing phase III randomized controlled trial. Patients with stage III/IV carcinoma of the larynx were randomized to either:

  1. Surgery (total laryngectomy) followed by postoperative radiation therapy (S+RT). Note: this was standard of care at the time of the trial.
  2. Induction chemotherapy (Cisplatin and 5-FU, 2 cycles). Patients were then re-evaluated. Patients with at least a partial response received a third cycle of chemotherapy(Cisplatin and 5-FU) followed by radiation therapy (CT+RT). If following radiation therapy they had a complete response, they received no further therapy and proceeded with follow-up. While those patients with partial response after radiation proceeded to salvage surgery (total laryngectomy). If following induction chemotherapy patients had less than a partial response they proceeded to surgery (total laryngectomy) followed by postoperative radiation therapy.

The results of the study with a median follow-up of 33 months:

  • 2-year overall survival: 68% S+RT vs. 68% CT+RT p=0.98
  • 2-year disease free survival: "Shorter in the chemotherapy groups, but not statistically significant" (Figure 2 in manuscript)
  • Distant metastatic disease: 17% S+RT vs. 11% CT+RT p=0.04

At four years follow-up:

  • Larynx preserved: 12% S+RT vs. 62% CT+RT (12% of patients had a partial laryngectomy)
  • Total laryngectomy: 88% S+RT vs. 38% CT+RT
  • Patients alive: 52% S+RT vs. 48% CT+RT
  • Patients alive with larynx: 5% S+RT vs. 31% CT+RT

T4 tumors also did worse than <T4 tumors. The salvage laryngectomy rate was 56% in T4 tumors vs. 29% in <T4 tumors p=0.001.

Incorrect Options:

Option B - Concurrent chemoradiation (cisplatin) versus surgery followed by postoperative radiation: This option does not match the design of the VA Larynx trial. The trial didn't compare surgery directly to concurrent chemoradiation with cisplatin. It instead focused on induction chemotherapy followed by radiation versus surgery followed by postoperative radiation.

Option C - Concurrent chemoradiation (cisplatin) versus induction chemotherapy (cisplatin/5-FU) followed by radiation versus radiation alone (three arms): This option also does not accurately represent the trial design. The VA Larynx trial had a two-arm design, comparing induction chemotherapy followed by radiation against surgery followed by postoperative radiation. It didn't involve a three-arm comparison that includes concurrent chemoradiation with cisplatin alone and radiation alone.

Option D - Concurrent chemoradiation (cisplatin/5-FU) versus radiation alone for resectable head and neck squamous cell carcinoma: This option is not aligned with the trial being discussed. The VA Larynx trial primarily focused on locally advanced laryngeal cancer, and the comparison was between induction chemotherapy followed by radiation and surgery followed by postoperative radiation. It did not include a comparison of concurrent chemoradiation (cisplatin/5-FU) versus radiation alone for resectable head and neck squamous cell carcinoma.

questions.stem: A 55-year-old male presents with a 2 cm, non- pruritic, non-ulcerating, erythematous plaque like lesion on the superior aspect of the chest, slowing increasing in size of the last 2 years, the biopsy from which confirmed primary cutaneous follicle center lymphoma (PCFCL). Which of the following would you recommend for the patient?
questions.stemHtml: A 55-year-old male presents with a 2 cm, non- pruritic, non-ulcerating, erythematous plaque like lesion on the superior aspect of the chest, slowing increasing in size of the last 2 years, the biopsy from which confirmed primary cutaneous follicle center lymphoma (PCFCL). Which of the following would you recommend for the patient?
questions.solution: Correct Option C - Radiation therapy Primary cutaneous follicle center lymphoma (PCFCL) is the most common form of primary cutaneous B-cell lymphoma (PCBCL) and represents ~ 60% of cases . Primary cutaneous follicle center lymphoma (PCFCL) most commonly present on the abdomen, chest, head, or neck. These lesions are typically less than <5 cm and solitary in nature. These lesions are typically non-ulcerating, erythematous plaque-like lesions which are painless and nonpruritic. These lesions typically have an indolent clinical course with an extended time period prior to definitive diagnosis.. As this is a B-cell neoplasm it is CD19, CD20, CD79a positive and CD5 negative. Genetically, they differ from nodal follicular lymphomas as they have variable (0-30%) expression of the BCL2 gene rearrangement and t(14;18) translocation. A unique genetic feature of PCFCL is amplification of the REL gene. Diagnosis of this entity is made on clinical suspicion and confirmed through pathological evaluation of (ideally) an excisional biopsy. Treatment for solitary (focal) lesions is generally radiation therapy (24-30 Gy) This recommendation is in agreement with NCCN guidelines and international guidelines. Incorrect Options: Option A - Multi-agent chemotherapy: Multi-agent chemotherapy refers to the use of multiple drugs to treat cancer. It's often used for aggressive cancers that require a systemic approach. In this case, primary cutaneous follicle center lymphoma (PCFCL) is a slow-growing type of non-Hodgkin lymphoma that primarily affects the skin. It's typically localized and has a relatively indolent course. Therefore, using aggressive multi-agent chemotherapy would be excessive and not the optimal choice for this patient. It could result in unnecessary side effects and potential harm. Option B- Rituximab: Rituximab is a monoclonal antibody that targets a specific protein on the surface of B cells, which are the cells involved in lymphoma. It is often used in the treatment of various lymphomas, including some cutaneous lymphomas. However, PCFCL is typically treated with localized approaches such as radiation therapy or surgical excision, especially for cases like the one described where the lesion is slow-growing and localized. Rituximab is more commonly used for lymphomas that involve deeper lymph nodes or are more systemic in nature. Option D - Surgical excision: Surgical excision involves removing the tumor or lesion through surgery. While surgical excision might be appropriate for certain cases of skin lymphomas, it's not usually the primary treatment choice for PCFCL. PCFCL tends to respond well to radiation therapy, which is a less invasive option. Surgical excision might be considered if the lesion is small and accessible, or if other treatments are contraindicated, but it's not the primary recommendation for PCFCL in most cases. @Neet_pg_bot

questions.stem: A 66-year-old male presents to his physician, with an enlarged right cervical lymph node, with no fevers, night sweats, or weight loss, undergoes a core needle biopsy which demonstrates polylobulated nuclei with laterally located nucleoli, the cells are found to be CD20+ and CD15-. He then undergoes a PET/CT which demonstrates hypermetabolic activity only within the right cervical neck. What is the recommended treatment for this patient?
questions.stemHtml: A 66-year-old male presents to his physician, with an enlarged right cervical lymph node, with no fevers, night sweats, or weight loss, undergoes a core needle biopsy which demonstrates polylobulated nuclei with laterally located nucleoli, the cells are found to be CD20+ and CD15-. He then undergoes a PET/CT which demonstrates hypermetabolic activity only within the right cervical neck. What is the recommended treatment for this patient?

options.label: A
options.text: ABVD x 2 cycles followed by 20 Gy involved-field radiation

options.label: D
options.text: Radiotherapy alone to 45 Gy (50.4 Gy if bulky)

questions.solution: Correct Option B - Radiotherapy alone 30-36 Gy: The patient in the vignette above demonstrates disease characteristics consistent with nodular lymphocyte predominant Hodgkin lymphoma (NLPHL). These cells classically are polylobulated nuclei with laterally located nucleoli ("popcorn cells") and are CD20+/CD15-. The recommended treatment for stage I/II nodular lymphocyte predominant Hodgkin lymphoma (NLPHL) is 30-36 Gy of radiotherapy alone. This is based on the current NCCN guidelines, as well the recent paper by Specht et al IJORBP 2014.There is not a role for chemotherapy in early stage NLPHL. Chen et al. JCO 2010 reviewed 113 stage I and II NLPHL patients. 93 patients treated with radiation alone, 13 with combined modality therapy, and 7 with chemotherapy alone. Progression-free survival (PFS) at 10 years was 85% and 61% for stage I and II, respectively. Overall survival (OS) was 94% and 97%. When analyzing control by radiation technique, no PFS or OS differences were seen between extended field radiation (EFRT), regional radiation, or limited field radiation. More second malignancy and cardiovascular deaths were seen with EFRT vs. limited field or regional radiation. Regarding the role of chemotherapy, 6 of 7 patients treated with chemotherapy alone as primary therapy failed, generally with early relapses. The addition of chemotherapy to radiation did not improve PFS but was associated with poorer OS. The duration of response associated with rituximab monotherapy is inferior to that with radiation alone. Incorrect Options: Option A - ABVD x 2 cycles followed by 20 Gy involved-field radiation: ABVD (Adriamycin, Bleomycin, Vinblastine, Dacarbazine) is a chemotherapy regimen commonly used for the treatment of Hodgkin lymphoma. However, in the given scenario, the patient's biopsy shows cells that are CD20+ and CD15-. This immunophenotype is more consistent with non-Hodgkin lymphoma, and ABVD is not the standard treatment for non-Hodgkin lymphoma. Option C - Rituximab monotherapy: Rituximab is a monoclonal antibody that targets CD20-positive B cells. It is commonly used in the treatment of B-cell non-Hodgkin lymphomas. However, in the case presented, the patient has lymph node enlargement and hypermetabolic activity in the right cervical neck, indicating localized disease. Rituximab monotherapy might not be sufficient to treat localized disease and may not be the standard treatment approach. Option D - Radiotherapy alone to 45 Gy (50.4 Gy if bulky): While radiotherapy is a standard treatment for localized non-Hodgkin lymphomas, the recommended dosage varies based on factors such as the type of lymphoma, its stage, and the presence of bulky disease. The given scenario does not mention the lymphoma subtype, and there is no indication of bulky disease. Therefore, using higher doses of radiation (45 Gy or 50.4 Gy) may not be necessary and could lead to unnecessary radiation exposure and potential side effects. @Neet_pg_bot

questions.stemHtml: A 3-day-old newborn was brought to the ER with gum bleeds . O/E he had moderate eczema covering about 40% of his body. The remainder of his exam is normal. Examination of the patient's blood smear demonstrates normal Hb and WBC, but a platelet count of 30,000 with the platelets present noted to be small. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.solution: Correct Option B - Wiskott-Aldrich Syndrome: The most likely diagnosis is Wiskott-Aldrich Syndrome.The patient's symptoms align with this syndrome, indicating a need for prompt diagnosis and management. Wiskott-Aldrich syndrome (WAS) is an X-linked hereditary disorder characterized by thrombocytopenia with small platelet size, eczema, and increased susceptibility to infections. As it is X-linked, it occurs more commonly in males, but is rare (~1-10 males per 1 million). Generally, patients present with easy bruising and/or petechiae. They may also experience GI bleeding and/or nosebleeds. Incorrect Options: Option A - Bernard-Soulier Syndrome: This is a rare inherited bleeding disorder characterized by a deficiency or dysfunction of the glycoprotein Ib-IX-V complex on the surface of platelets. It leads to large platelets and a decreased ability of platelets to bind to von Willebrand factor, resulting in bleeding tendencies. In the scenario described, the patient's platelets were noted to be small, which is not consistent with Bernard-Soulier Syndrome. Option C - Hemophilia A: Hemophilia A is a bleeding disorder caused by a deficiency of clotting factor VIII. It is an X-linked recessive disorder that primarily affects males. While it can cause significant bleeding, the symptoms in this case, such as eczema and small platelets, are not consistent with hemophilia A. Option D - Glanzman's Thrombasthenia: Glanzman's Thrombasthenia is a rare inherited disorder characterized by a deficiency or dysfunction of the platelet glycoprotein IIb/IIIa complex, which is essential for platelet aggregation. It typically presents with mucocutaneous bleeding, but in this case, the patient's platelet count is low (thrombocytopenia), which is not a typical feature of Glanzman's Thrombasthenia. @Neet_pg_bot

questions.stem: What were the chemotherapy agents used in the adjuvant chemotherapy arm of GOG 122 (Randall et al JCO 2006), the phase III trial of stage III or IV endometrial carcinoma?
questions.stemHtml: What were the chemotherapy agents used in the adjuvant chemotherapy arm of GOG 122 (Randall et al JCO 2006), the phase III trial of stage III or IV endometrial carcinoma?
questions.solution: Correct Option D - Cisplatin and Doxorubicin: GOG 122 (Randall et al JCO 2006) sought to compare the efficacy of adjuvant whole-abdominal irradiation versus adjuvant chemotherapy for locally advanced, optimally debulked endometrial cancer, which had previously never been compared in a prospective, randomized trial. The study enrolled 422 patients with stage III or IV endometrial carcinoma of any histology who had undergone total abdominal hysterectomy, bilateral salpingo-oophorectomy, and optimal debulking with less than 2 cm of residual gross disease remaining at any one site. Lymph node sampling was optional. Following surgery, patients were randomized to: Adjuvant whole-abdominal radiation Adjuvant chemotherapy (chemotherapy was doxorubicin (60 mg/m 2 ) and cisplatin (50 mg/m2), administered every 3 weeks for 7 total cycles, followed by 1 additional cycle of cisplatin alone. The maximum allowable cumulative dose of doxorubicin was 420 mg/m 2 ). The primary endpoint of the study was progression-free survival, with overall survival as a secondary endpoint. At median follow-up of 74 months: 5-year progression-free survival was 38% for the whole-abdominal irradiation arm vs. 50% for the chemotherapy arm (p=0.007). 5-year overall survival was 42% for the whole-abdominal irradiation arm vs. 55% for the chemotherapy arm (p=0.004). The patients receiving chemotherapy experienced more grade 3-4 hematologic and gastrointestinal toxicity, as compared with the patients receiving whole-abdominal irradiation. The study authors concluded that chemotherapy improved progression-free survival and overall survival as compared to whole-abdominal irradiation. This trial played a role in establishing the role of adjuvant chemotherapy for patients with advanced or high risk disease. However, please note that the NCCN Guidelines recommends a regimen of carboplatin and taxol for non-sarcoma endometrial cancers (or carboplatin, taxol, and herceptin for HER2-positive uterine serous carcinomas). Incorrect Options: Option A - Carboplatin: Carboplatin is a chemotherapy agent commonly used to treat various types of cancer, including ovarian cancer. However, in the context of the GOG 122 trial, the combination of Carboplatin alone was not the adjuvant chemotherapy regimen used. Option B - Carboplatin and Paclitaxel: Carboplatin and Paclitaxel is a common chemotherapy regimen used in various gynecologic cancers, including ovarian cancer. However, in the context of the GOG 122 trial, this specific combination was not the adjuvant chemotherapy regimen used. Option C - Cisplatin: Cisplatin is a chemotherapy drug used to treat various types of cancer, but it was not used alone as the adjuvant chemotherapy regimen in the GOG 122 trial for stage III or IV endometrial carcinoma. @Neet_pg_bot

Correct Option D - Cisplatin and Doxorubicin:

GOG 122 (Randall et al JCO 2006) sought to compare the efficacy of adjuvant whole-abdominal irradiation versus adjuvant chemotherapy for locally advanced, optimally debulked endometrial cancer, which had previously never been compared in a prospective, randomized trial.

The study enrolled 422 patients with stage III or IV endometrial carcinoma of any histology who had undergone total abdominal hysterectomy, bilateral salpingo-oophorectomy, and optimal debulking with less than 2 cm of residual gross disease remaining at any one site. Lymph node sampling was optional. Following surgery, patients were randomized to:

  • Adjuvant whole-abdominal radiation
  • Adjuvant chemotherapy (chemotherapy was doxorubicin (60 mg/m2) and cisplatin (50 mg/m2), administered every 3 weeks for 7 total cycles, followed by 1 additional cycle of cisplatin alone. The maximum allowable cumulative dose of doxorubicin was 420 mg/m2 ).

The primary endpoint of the study was progression-free survival, with overall survival as a secondary endpoint. At median follow-up of 74 months:

  • 5-year progression-free survival was 38% for the whole-abdominal irradiation arm vs. 50% for the chemotherapy arm (p=0.007).
  • 5-year overall survival was 42% for the whole-abdominal irradiation arm vs. 55% for the chemotherapy arm (p=0.004).

The patients receiving chemotherapy experienced more grade 3-4 hematologic and gastrointestinal toxicity, as compared with the patients receiving whole-abdominal irradiation. The study authors concluded that chemotherapy improved progression-free survival and overall survival as compared to whole-abdominal irradiation.

This trial played a role in establishing the role of adjuvant chemotherapy for patients with advanced or high risk disease. However, please note that the NCCN Guidelines recommends a regimen of carboplatin and taxol for non-sarcoma endometrial cancers (or carboplatin, taxol, and herceptin for HER2-positive uterine serous carcinomas).

questions.stem: A 54-year-old woman with bleeding per rectum underwent colonoscopy which revealed a mass in the transverse colon. She undergoes partial colectomy and is found on surgery to have a stage II colon adenocarcinoma. She is referred by her surgeon to your OPD seeking opinion for adjuvant therapy. Which of the following would be most likely to convince you NOT to recommend adjuvant therapy in this case?
questions.stemHtml: A 54-year-old woman with bleeding per rectum underwent colonoscopy which revealed a mass in the transverse colon. She undergoes partial colectomy and is found on surgery to have a stage II colon adenocarcinoma. She is referred by her surgeon to your OPD seeking opinion for adjuvant therapy. Which of the following would be most likely to convince you NOT to recommend adjuvant therapy in this case?
questions.solution: Correct Option D - Evidence of microsatellite instability: Patients with stage III colon cancer clearly benefit from adjuvant chemotherapy so long as they are healthy enough to tolerate it well and have no contraindications. Patients with resected stage II disease, on the other hand, face a much more nuanced and difficult choice. It is clear from multiple studies that while there are a small number of patients with stage II disease who are likely to benefit from adjuvant therapy, the majority of patients likely do NOT benefit and so the prudence of offering chemotherapy to all patients in this setting is questionable. There is some agreement that patients should be stratified into "high risk" (of recurrence) and "low risk" of recurrence, but there is a lack of agreement as to what factors qualify patients to be in either camp. One thing that has become clear over time, however, is that patients who have microsatellite unstable disease are much less likely to have disease recurrence and, therefore, in the absence of other risk factors that are concerning, there is general consensus that patients who have microsatellite unstable disease are recommended to NOT receive chemotherapy. Microsatellite instability can be measured in multiple different ways, but in general IHC looking for the protein products of the most commonly mutated genes is the fastest and thus the most used. While the concordance between this and more involved methods of testing is not perfect, it is generally above 90% and thus this is accepted as a reasonable screening mechanism so long as there are no clinical factors to suggest that a patient is likely to be microsatellite unstable. Incorrect Options: Option A - pT4 disease: This refers to the pathological staging of the tumor. "pT4" indicates that the tumor has invaded through the serosa (the outermost layer of the colon wall) and possibly into surrounding structures. Tumor staging is an important factor in deciding treatment strategies. In general, more advanced stages of cancer are associated with a higher likelihood of recurrence and worse outcomes. Given that this patient already has stage II disease, which implies localized involvement without distant metastasis, having pT4 disease suggests a more advanced extent of invasion. This would actually make adjuvant therapy more likely to be recommended, as the tumor is considered higher risk due to its extent of invasion. Option B - Lack of perineural invasion: Perineural invasion refers to cancer cells invading the nerves present in the vicinity of the tumor. This is a negative prognostic factor and indicates a higher risk of tumor recurrence and spread. If the patient lacked perineural invasion, it could be considered a favorable prognostic factor. However, this would not be a convincing reason to avoid adjuvant therapy. Adjuvant therapy is often recommended precisely to reduce the risk of recurrence, especially in cases of stage II colon cancer where the risk of recurrence is moderate. Option C - Tumor rupture: Tumor rupture refers to the tumor breaking through the wall of the colon, potentially releasing cancer cells into the abdominal cavity. This is generally associated with a higher risk of cancer spreading and recurrence. In the context of a patient with stage II colon adenocarcinoma, tumor rupture would be a concerning feature that might actually lean towards recommending adjuvant therapy, rather than not recommending it @Neet_pg_bot

questions.stem: A 52-year-old woman was seen in haematology clinic due to elevated ferritin. She was recently diagnosed with hypothyroidism and has been taking levothyroxine regularly. She had menopause at the age of 45. No family history of hemochromatosis. She is otherwise asymptomatic without any signs of cirrhosis liver or congestive heart failure. Laboratory studies are summarized below. CBC: WBC 6,000/uL, Hb- 14.7 g/dL, MCV 88 FL, platelet count 200,000/uL. BMP: Normal Random Blood Glucose: 90 mg/dL LFTS: Normal. Iron studies: ferritin 975 ng/mL, serum iron 234 ug/dL, iron binding capacity 265 ug/dL and transferrin saturation 60%. HFE genotyping revealed homozygous C282Y genotype. What treatment option would you recommend?
questions.stemHtml:
A 52-year-old woman was seen in haematology clinic due to elevated ferritin. She was recently diagnosed with hypothyroidism and has been taking levothyroxine regularly. She had menopause at the age of 45. No family history of hemochromatosis. She is otherwise asymptomatic without any signs of cirrhosis liver or congestive heart failure. Laboratory studies are summarized below.
CBC: WBC 6,000/uL, Hb- 14.7 g/dL, MCV 88 FL, platelet count 200,000/uL.
BMP: Normal
Random Blood Glucose: 90 mg/dL
LFTS: Normal.
Iron studies: ferritin 975 ng/mL, serum iron 234 ug/dL, iron binding capacity 265 ug/dL and transferrin saturation 60%.
HFE genotyping revealed homozygous C282Y genotype.
What treatment option would you recommend?

options.label: B
options.text: Hepatic MRI to determine liver iron content

questions.solution: Correct Option D - Weekly phlebotomy: Hereditary hemochromatosis is a genetic disorder characterized by systemic iron overload. It principally affects individuals of northern European ancestry, most commonly due to HFE mutations (type 1 hereditary hemochromatosis or HFE hemochromatosis). The major HFE mutation is C282Y, and approximately 15% of individuals of the northern European origin are heterozygotes and 0.5% are homozygotes. C282Y heterozygotes do not develop disease. Approximately two-thirds of homozygotes for C282Y develop iron overload with elevated ferritin and markedly high transferrin saturation. Other HFE mutations are H63D and S65C. Compound heterozygotes (C282Y/H63D) may also develop hemochromatosis, but far less likely. The effect of S65C mutation is very minimal. HFE hemochromatosis is generally diagnosed in fifth or sixth decade of life (in women after menopause). Clinical symptoms include fatigue, loss of libido, abdominal pain and arthralgia. Cirrhosis of the liver, cardiomyopathy, diabetes and endocrine dysfunction are frequent due organ damage from iron accumulation. The fully penetrant form of the disease (bronze diabetes) is rarely seen. Treatment of HFE hemochromatosis in C282Y homozygotes is weekly phlebotomy to remove accumulated iron. Removal of 500 ml of blood removes approximately 200 mg iron. Phlebotomy is recommended in individuals with iron overload even in the absence of end organ damage. The goal is to reduce the ferritin to <100 ng/mL. Observation can be considered in C282Y homozygotes if the serum ferritin is normal or moderately elevated. In patients with markedly elevated ferritin, observation is not appropriate even in the absence of end organ damage. Incorrect Options: Option A - Observation: This option is not recommended for hereditary hemochromatosis with elevated ferritin levels. Left untreated, hereditary hemochromatosis can lead to iron overload, which may result in various complications such as liver cirrhosis, diabetes, and heart problems. Active intervention is necessary to manage iron levels. Option B - Hepatic MRI to determine liver iron content: While MRI can be used to estimate liver iron content, it is not the first-line treatment for hereditary hemochromatosis. MRI can help monitor iron overload and guide treatment decisions, but it is not the primary therapeutic approach. Option C - Oral deferasirox: Deferasirox is an iron chelator that can be used to manage iron overload. However, in cases of hereditary hemochromatosis, especially with high ferritin levels, phlebotomy (removing blood to lower iron levels) is generally the preferred initial treatment. Deferasirox might be considered in specific cases where phlebotomy is not feasible or well-tolerated. @Neet_pg_bot

His labs show a WBC of 44,000, hemoglobin of 10.4 g/dL and platelets of 100,000. Kidney and liver function are unremarkable. He has noted some fatigue over the last year as well. He agrees to start treatment with acalabrutinib plus obinutuzumab. Which of the listed trials showed efficacy of this combination regimen versus acalabrutinib monotherapy?
questions.stemHtml: A 55-year-old gentleman with non-17p deleted CLL is referred to with few palpable inguinal lymph nodes and splenomegaly. His labs show a WBC of 44,000, hemoglobin of 10.4 g/dL and platelets of 100,000. Kidney and liver function are unremarkable. He has noted some fatigue over the last year as well. He agrees to start treatment with acalabrutinib plus obinutuzumab. Which of the listed trials showed efficacy of this combination regimen versus acalabrutinib monotherapy?
questions.solution: Correct Option A - ELEVATE-TN: The phase 3 trial ELEVATE-TN was a randomized phase 3 clinical trial in previously untreated CLL patients, comparing acalabrutinib with obinutuzumab vs chlorambucil + obinutuzumab vs acalabrutinib monotherapy. At the first interim analysis, with a median follow-up of 28 months, the median progression-free survival was not reached in both acalabrutinib arms versus 22.6 months in the control arm. Hazard ratio 0.10. P< 0.001. Overall response rates were 94% versus 79% versus 86% in the monotherapy arm. Grade ≥ 3 AE occurred in 70.2% of patients in the acalabrutinib + obinutuzumab group , 69.8% of the obinutuzumab chlorambucil group and 49.7% of the acalabrutinib monotherapy group. Incorrect Options: Option B - PACE: The PACE trial studied the efficacy of ibrutinib, not acalabrutinib. Ibrutinib is another Bruton's tyrosine kinase (BTK) inhibitor used in CLL treatment. Therefore, this trial is not relevant to the combination regimen involving acalabrutinib and obinutuzumab. Option C - EMRACA: The EMRACA trial did not involve either acalabrutinib or obinutuzumab. Instead, it evaluated the use of the PARP inhibitor talazoparib in patients with germline BRCA-mutated HER2-negative advanced breast cancer. This trial is unrelated to the combination regimen mentioned in the question. Option D - MABLE: There is no known trial by the name "MABLE" that relates to CLL treatment or the mentioned combination regimen. questions.solution: Correct Option D - Compensated respiratory acidosis: The elevated PaCO 2 and low pH indicate respiratory acidosis , likely due to the patient's underlying COPD. However, the increased HCO 3 - suggests that the patient's kidneys have compensated for the respiratory acidosis by retaining bicarbonate ions , increasing the serum bicarbonate concentration. It results in a pH within the normal range despite the elevated PaCO2 , indicating compensated respiratory acidosis. Incorrect Options: Option A - Respiratory acidosis: An elevated PaCO2 and a decreased pH characterize respiratory acidosis. In this case, however, the increased HCO3 - suggests that the patient's kidneys have compensated for the respiratory acidosis by retaining bicarbonate ions , increasing the serum bicarbonate concentration. Option B - Respiratory alkalosis: A decreased PaCO2 and an increased pH characterize respiratory alkalosis. This can be caused by hyperventilation, such as anxiety or panic attacks, pulmonary embolism, or high altitude. This patient's arterial blood gas analysis shows an elevated PaCO2 and a decreased pH, inconsistent with respiratory alkalosis. Option C - Metabolic acidosis: Metabolic acidosis is characterized by a decreased HCO3- and a decreased pH . Several conditions, including diabetic ketoacidosis, lactic acidosis, or renal failure, can cause this. While a patient with COPD may develop metabolic acidosis in certain situations, such as when they develop respiratory failure, and their compensatory mechanisms are overwhelmed. questions.stemHtml: A 35-year-old male with Anti-GBM Disease receives initial treatment with plasma exchange and steroids, but his renal function continues declining despite therapy. What is the next best treatment option for this patient?
questions.solution: Correct Option A - Rituximab: Rituximab is a monoclonal antibody that targets and depletes B cells responsible for producing autoantibodies in Anti-GBM Disease. Research has indicated that rituximab can induce remission in people with Anti-GBM Disease who have not responded to initial treatment with plasma exchange and steroids. Rituximab is generally well-tolerated, with infusion responses being the most common adverse effect, and it has a lower chance of generating infections and other problems than Cyclophosphamide. Incorrect Options: Option B - Cyclophosphamide: Cyclophosphamide is an alkylating agent that targets rapidly dividing cells, including immune cells. It is commonly used in treating autoimmune disorders, including Anti-GBM Disease, to suppress the immune response and prevent the production of new autoantibodies. When combined with plasma exchange and steroids, Cyclophosphamide can produce remission in patients with Anti-GBM Disease. However, Cyclophosphamide has more side effects than rituximab and is generally reserved for patients who cannot tolerate or have not responded to rituximab therapy. Cyclophosphamide side effects can include bone marrow suppression, gastrointestinal toxicity, bladder toxicity, and an increased risk of infections and cancer. Therefore, while Cyclophosphamide may be used to treat Anti-GBM Disease, it is not the next best treatment option for a patient not responding to initial therapy with plasma exchange and steroids. Rituximab has been demonstrated to be successful in producing remission in individuals who have not responded to early therapy. It is generally well-tolerated with a lower risk of problems than Cyclophosphamide. Option C - Intravenous immunoglobulin (IVIG): IVIG is a mixture of antibodies derived from pooled plasma used to treat various autoimmune and infectious disorders. IVIG has been used as an adjunctive therapy in some cases of Anti-GBM Disease, but its efficacy is unclear, and it is not considered a standard treatment. A case report described the successful use of IVIG in a patient with Anti-GBM Disease who was refractory to plasma exchange and steroids. However, more extensive studies are needed to establish its effectiveness. IVIG is expensive and can have significant side effects, including infusion reactions, thrombosis, and renal failure. Therefore, while IVIG may be used in some cases of Anti-GBM Disease, it is not the next best treatment option for a patient not responding to initial therapy with plasma exchange and steroids. Rituximab has been demonstrated to be beneficial in producing remission in individuals who have not responded to early therapy. It is generally well-tolerated with a reduced risk of problems than IVIG. Option D - Mycophenolate mofetil (MMF): MMF is an immunosuppressive agent commonly used to treat autoimmune disorders, including lupus nephritis and vasculitis. Limited data exist on the use of MMF in Anti-GBM Disease, and it is not considered a standard treatment. One case report described the successful use of MMF in combination with plasma exchange and steroids in a patient with Anti-GBM Disease. However, more extensive studies are needed to establish its efficacy. MMF can have significant side effects, including gastrointestinal symptoms, infections, and bone marrow suppression. questions.stem: A 25-year-old man presents to the clinic with complaints of muscle weakness, fatigue, and frequent episodes of vomiting. He reports that he has been experiencing these symptoms for the past six months, and they have been getting progressively worse. He denies any history of hypertension, diabetes, or kidney disease. The patient's family history is significant for a sister with a similar illness. On physical examination, he is found to be hypotensive with a blood pressure of 90/60 mmHg. The patient appears dehydrated with dry mucous membranes. The examination of the chest and cardiovascular system is normal. The abdomen is soft and non-tender, and there is no hepatosplenomegaly. The patient has generalized muscle weakness, and the deep tendon reflexes are diminished. Laboratory investigations show hypokalemia, metabolic alkalosis, and normal renal function. A renal ultrasound reveals normal-sized kidneys with no evidence of obstruction or stones. A diagnosis of type 4A Bartter syndrome is made. What is the most likely management for this syndrome?

A renal ultrasound reveals normal-sized kidneys with no evidence of obstruction or stones. A diagnosis of type 4A Bartter syndrome is made. What is the most likely management for this syndrome?
questions.solution: Correct Option A - Oral potassium supplementation: This disorder is characterized by hypokalemia, which occurs by impaired potassium secretion in the distal tubules of the kidneys. By supplementing oral potassium, the patient's hypokalemia can be corrected. It occurs by mutations in the gene encoding the barttin subunit of the chloride channel in the renal tubules. This results in impaired chloride reabsorption and potassium secretion in the distal tubules, leading to hypokalemia and metabolic alkalosis. Clinical Features: symptoms of hypokalemia, such as muscle weakness, fatigue, and cramping with: Dehydration Polyuria and polydipsia Nausea and vomiting Growth retardation (in children) Lab Investigations Hypokalemia Metabolic alkalosis Hyper-reninemia Normal renal function Genetic Testing: this can confirm the diagnosis of type 4A Bartter syndrome by identifying mutations in the gene encoding the barttin subunit of the chloride channel in the renal tubules. Imaging Findings: Renal ultrasound may show normal-sized kidneys with no evidence of obstruction or stones. Treatment Options: Oral potassium supplementation is the mainstay of treatment for hypokalemia. NSAID s are used to reduce prostaglandin synthesis, which increases potassium secretion in the distal tubules. ACE inhibitors or ARBs may be used to reduce hyper-reninemia and prevent renal damage. Genetic counseling is offered to affected individuals and their families. Option B: Intravenous potassium chloride infusion It can cause complications such as hyperkalemia and venous irritation. It is typically reserved for severe cases of hypokalemia or in emergencies where the patient cannot tolerate oral potassium supplementation . It is given in: Severe hypokalemia with serum potassium levels <2.5 mmol/L Cardiac arrhythmias or other life-threatening complications due to severe hypokalemia Unable to tolerate oral potassium supplements , which can occur in cases of ileus or vomiting. Option C: Loop diuretics They prevent salt and chloride from being reabsorbed in the thick ascending limb of the loop of Henle, which can lead to an increase in potassium and hydrogen ion excretion and exacerbate hypokalemia and metabolic alkalosis . It may be useful in conditions where sodium and fluid retention are prominent features, such as edema and heart failure. Hypercalcemia, it can increase calcium excretion in the urine and decrease the risk of kidney stone formation. In nephrotic syndrome, it can help to reduce edema and fluid overload . Option D: Sodium restriction It has the potential to exacerbate the underlying electrolyte imbalance . It can disrupt the sodium-potassium exchange in the distal tubules, leading to further potassium loss and metabolic alkalosis . It may be difficult to achieve in some patients and can lead to dehydration and other complications. It may be appropriate in conditions where sodium retention is a prominent feature, such as heart failure or edema, as well as in hypertension and chronic kidney disease . @Neet_pg_bot

An ECG shows diffuse ST-segment elevations. An echocardiogram reveals pericardial effusion. Laboratory tests reveal a serum creatinine level of 3.2 mg/dL, BUN of 50 mg/dL, and an elevated C-reactive protein level. What is the most appropriate next step in the management of this patient?
questions.stemHtml: A 55-year-old male with a history of CKD presents to the emergency department with shortness of breath and chest pain. Physical examination reveals a pericardial friction rub. An ECG shows diffuse ST-segment elevations. An echocardiogram reveals pericardial effusion. Laboratory tests reveal a serum creatinine level of 3.2 mg/dL, BUN of 50 mg/dL, and an elevated C-reactive protein level. What is the most appropriate next step in the management of this patient?

options.label: A
options.text: Immediate pericardiocentesis to relieve cardiac tamponade

options.label: C

options.label: D

questions.answerText: Start hemodialysis to lower serum urea levels
questions.solution: Correct Option C - Start hemodialysis to lower serum urea levels: Uremic pericarditis is a common complication of advanced chronic kidney disease (CKD). It is caused by the accumulation of waste products in the blood, such as urea, which can irritate the pericardium (the sac that surrounds the heart). The condition is characterized by inflammation and fluid accumulation in the pericardial space, which can lead to cardiac tamponade and compromise the heart's function. Clinical presentation of uremic pericarditis can include chest pain, shortness of breath, cough, and fever . A pericardial friction rub may be heard on auscultation of the chest. ECG changes may include diffuse ST-segment elevations , and an echocardiogram can confirm the presence of pericardial effusion . Managing uremic pericarditis involves addressing the condition's underlying cause, which is the accumulation of waste products in the blood due to impaired renal function. The primary treatment for uremic pericarditis is hemodialysis, which helps to lower the serum urea levels and relieve the irritation of the pericardium . Hemodialysis should be initiated promptly in patients with symptomatic uremic pericarditis to prevent complications such as cardiac tamponade. In addition to hemodialysis, other treatments may be considered to manage the symptoms of uremic pericarditis. Pericardiocentesis may be necessary to relieve cardiac tamponade in severe cases, and nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs) or colchicine may be used to reduce inflammation and pain. Corticosteroids may also be considered in some cases, although they are generally reserved for refractory cases due to potentially adverse effects. In cases where uremic pericarditis is recurrent or refractory to medical management, pericardial stripping surgery may be considered . This procedure involves removing the pericardium and can provide long-term relief of symptoms in select patients. Incorrect Options: Option A - Immediate pericardiocentesis to relieve cardiac tamponade: Pericardiocentesis may be necessary for the presence of cardiac tamponade, but it is not the first-line treatment for uremic pericarditis. Option B - Initiate treatment with oral prednisone: Corticosteroids may also be considered in some cases, although they are generally reserved for refractory cases due to potentially adverse effects. Option D - Refer the patient to a cardiac surgeon for pericardial stripping: Cardiac surgery may be considered in refractory cases but is not the first-line treatment option. @Neet_pg_bot

questions.stem: A 42-year-old male presents to the medical outpatient department due to fatigue and weight gain for the last 2 months. He has had a history of HIV/AIDS for the last 15 years. Physical examination reveals generalised oedema. Urinalysis shows proteinuria in the range of nephrotic syndrome. Further investigations show non-specific immune deposits trapped in focal scars. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.stemHtml: A 42-year-old male presents to the medical outpatient department due to fatigue and weight gain for the last 2 months. He has had a history of HIV/AIDS for the last 15 years. Physical examination reveals generalised oedema. Urinalysis shows proteinuria in the range of nephrotic syndrome. Further investigations show non-specific immune deposits trapped in focal scars. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.solution: Correct Option A - Focal segmental glomerular sclerosis (FSGS): The patient presents with fatigue, weight gain, generalised oedema, a history of HIV/AIDS, proteinuria, and non-specific immune deposits trapped in focal scars indicating a diagnosis of FSGS. FSGS causes 40% of nephrotic syndrome cases in adults and 20% in children. It is one of the most common causes of primary glomerulopathy in adults . FSGS results in sclerosing of some glomeruli, and each glomerulus is only partially affected. It can be primary or secondary . Adults present with proteinuria, hypertension, hypoalbuminemia, oedema, microscopic haematuria, or renal insufficiency. Children present with full-blown nephrotic syndrome. Oedema develops over a few weeks, abruptly increasing the weight by 15-20 pounds. On histopathology, FSGS presents with sclerosis, hyalinosis, and synechiae formation. This results in segmental occlusion of glomerular capillaries . Effacement of foot processes is a significant finding on electron microscopy. No abnormalities of the basement membrane are seen. Immunofluorescence shows non-specific immune deposits (IgM and C3) trapped in focal scars. Incorrect Options: Option B - IgA nephropathy: IgA nephropathy is another one of the most common glomerulopathies in young adults. It presents with haematuria as the earliest sign a few days after an upper respiratory tract infection. Proteinuria may occur later. Slow progressive loss of renal function leads to end-stage renal disease (ESRD). Mesangial deposits of IgA are seen on immunofluorescence. As these features are absent, it is an unlikely diagnosis in this patient. Option C - Membranous glomerulonephritis: Membranous glomerulonephritis is the most common cause of nephrotic syndrome in adults. It is associated with malignancies, heavy metal poisoning, certain drugs, and infections. Granular subepithelial deposits of IgG are seen on immunofluorescence. As these features are absent, it is an unlikely diagnosis in this patient. Option D - Minimal change disease: Minimal change disease can occur in all ages but most commonly in children as nephrotic syndrome. It easily remits with corticosteroid therapy. It is associated with atopies, HLA-DR7, and certain drugs . No immune deposits are seen on immunofluorescence. As these features are absent, it is an unlikely diagnosis in this patient. @Neet_pg_bot

questions.solution: Correct Option D - Autosomal dominant polycystic kidney disease: Autosomal dominant polycystic kidney disease (ADPKD) is the most common hereditary kidney disease, affecting approximately 1 in 500 to 1,000 people worldwide. The condition is caused by mutations in the PKD1 or PKD2 genes , which encode for proteins polycystin-1 and polycystin-2 , respectively. These proteins are involved in the regulation of tubular epithelial cell proliferation, differentiation, and apoptosis. In ADPKD, the affected individuals develop multiple cysts in their kidneys, which gradually enlarge and replace normal renal parenchyma, leading to chronic kidney disease, hypertension , and eventually end-stage renal disease (ESRD). Cysts can also develop in other organs, including the liver, pancreas, and spleen. The inheritance pattern of ADPKD is autosomal dominant , meaning that only one copy of the mutated gene is sufficient to cause the disease. Therefore, affected individuals have a 50% chance of passing the mutation on to each of their offspring. In the given scenario, the patient has a mutation in the PKD1 gene , the most commonly mutated gene in ADPKD, accounting for approximately 85% of cases. ARPKD typically presents in infancy or early childhood , with symptoms such as enlarged kidneys, liver fibrosis, and hypertension.
